shard.title: The British Isles and Europe
shard.author: regional historian: British Isles and Europe
shard.note: Ireland, the crown dependencies, the metropole itself, and every European and North Atlantic possession Britain held, traded, sold, occupied or abandoned. Non-British-Isles territories carry region mediterranean because the region vocabulary has no separate value for continental Europe or the North Atlantic; each carries an honest subregion.

territories.name: Great Britain
territories.formalName: The Kingdom of England and Wales, then the Kingdom of Great Britain, then the United Kingdom

namesOverTime.name: Kingdom of England
namesOverTime.note: Wales was annexed to it by statute in 1536 and had no separate legal existence again until 1999.

namesOverTime.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
namesOverTime.note: The state kept the old name for five years after the Free State left; the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927 changed it to 'Northern Ireland'.

namesOverTime.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

modernSuccessors.name: United Kingdom
modernSuccessors.note: Scotland and Wales have had their own parliaments again since 1999; a Scottish independence referendum in 2014 voted 55.3% to 44.7% to remain.

from.note: The Statute of Rhuddlan, issued in March 1284, put the conquered Welsh principality under English law and English sheriffs.

geoCoverage.label: England and the conquered Wales
geoCoverage.change: Edward I's conquest of Gwynedd in 1282-83 attached Wales to the English crown; the marcher lordships kept their own courts until 1536.

geoCoverage.label: Great Britain
geoCoverage.change: The Scottish and English parliaments each passed an Act of Union and dissolved themselves into one parliament at Westminster.

date.note: The war ended in 1283; the Statute of Rhuddlan that settled the government of Wales is dated March 1284.

acquisitions.how: Edward I invaded Gwynedd twice, killed Llywelyn ap Gruffudd near Builth in December 1282, had his brother Dafydd hanged, drawn and quartered at Shrewsbury, and ringed the conquest with castles at Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris paid for by English taxes.

counterparties.name: The Principality of Gwynedd and the Welsh kingdoms
counterparties.lost: Their independence and their dynasty. Llywelyn's head was carried to London and displayed at the Tower, and the walled boroughs planted beside the new castles barred Welsh people from trading or holding office inside them.
counterparties.note: The bars on Welsh residence and office-holding in the new boroughs were real and long-lasting, and were tightened again by the penal statutes of 1401-02.

instrument.name: Statute of Rhuddlan (the Statute of Wales)
instrument.note: Strictly a royal ordinance rather than an act of parliament; it is conventionally called a statute.

people.name: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd
people.role: last native Prince of Wales; killed at Cilmeri in December 1282

people.name: Dafydd ap Gruffydd
people.role: his brother; the first man recorded as hanged, drawn and quartered for treason

people.name: Edward I
people.role: commanded the conquest and built the castles that held it

acquisitions.resistance: Owain Glyndwr's rising of 1400-1415 held most of Wales, summoned a parliament at Machynlleth and made treaties with France before it was starved out; the penal laws Parliament passed against Welsh people in reply stayed on the books for over a century.

date.note: The Laws in Wales Act was passed in the 1535 session and took effect in 1536; both years are used.

acquisitions.how: Henry VIII's Laws in Wales Acts abolished the marcher lordships, divided Wales into counties that sent MPs to Westminster, and made English the only language of the courts, so that no monoglot Welsh speaker could hold office in Wales.

counterparties.name: The Welsh marcher lordships and Welsh law
counterparties.lost: Cyfraith Hywel, the Welsh law of inheritance and compensation, was abolished in favour of English common law, and Welsh was shut out of every court and public office for four centuries.

acquisitions.how: The Scottish parliament voted itself out of existence on 25 March 1707 and merged with the English one at Westminster, where Scotland held 45 of 558 Commons seats; the vote followed the ruin of Scotland's own colony at Darien and an English act threatening Scottish trade.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Scotland
counterparties.lost: Its parliament and its separate crown, in exchange for free trade with England and its colonies and a payment of £398,085 10s. — the 'Equivalent' — much of which went to men who had lost money at Darien.
counterparties.note: Scotland kept its own law, church and universities, and still has them. That is why the Union is not simply an annexation.

instrument.name: Treaty of Union, enacted as the Union with England Act 1707 and the Union with Scotland Act 1706
instrument.note: The commissioners agreed the treaty in July 1706; each parliament then ratified it, and the Union took effect on 1 May 1707.

people.name: James Douglas, 2nd Duke of Queensberry
people.role: Queen's Commissioner who managed the Union through the Scottish parliament

people.name: Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun
people.role: led the parliamentary opposition to the Union

people.name: William Paterson
people.role: founder of the Bank of England and of the failed Darien colony that made the Union financially attractive

acquisitions.resistance: There were anti-Union riots in Edinburgh, Glasgow and Dumfries in 1706, addresses against the Union from most of the shires and burghs that petitioned, and Jacobite risings in 1708, 1715, 1719 and 1745.

contested.note: Whether the Union was bought — Robert Burns wrote of Scots 'bought and sold for English gold' — or was a rational bargain after Darien is still argued. So is whether Scotland belongs in an atlas of empire at all, given that Scots went on to supply a share of the empire's governors, soldiers, doctors and planters far larger than their share of Britain's population.

statusPeriods.label: The Kingdom of England, with Wales annexed
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The king in London ruled England directly and Wales through a Council in the Marches at Ludlow; from 1536 Welsh counties sent MPs to the English parliament and English was the only language of the law.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Westminster, and for Wales the Council in the Marches at Ludlow
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise. Something like one adult man in ten could vote in a county election, and no women could vote at all.
statusPeriods.note: The label is deliberately anachronistic: there was no United Kingdom before 1707. This atlas uses 'part-of-uk' to mean the metropolitan state itself — the place the orders came from — and says so here rather than inventing a category.

statusPeriods.label: The state that ran the empire
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: One parliament at Westminster legislated for Britain, and from 1801 for Ireland; colonial governors answered to a Secretary of State in London, from 1854 through a Colonial Office that at its height had fewer staff than a large school.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Westminster and Whitehall
statusPeriods.franchise: Roughly 3% of adults could vote in 1831. The Reform Acts of 1832, 1867 and 1884 widened it; women over 30 got the vote in 1918 and all adults in 1928 — after most of the empire had been conquered.
statusPeriods.note: Scotland and Wales gained devolved legislatures in 1999. Neither is independent; both have a parliament again for the first time since 1707 and 1536.

stillBritish.note: England, Scotland and Wales are the United Kingdom, with about 65 million people; Scotland voted 55.3% to 44.7% against independence in 2014 and both Scotland and Wales have had devolved parliaments since 1999.

populationTransfer.note: Britain exported people as well as goods: about 10 million people left the United Kingdom for the empire and the United States between 1815 and 1914, and Scotland and Ireland sent the highest shares of their populations.

slavery.note: British ships carried about 3.4 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, more than any other nation in the eighteenth century, and Parliament then abolished the trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833.

emancipationDate.note: Full freedom came only on 1 August 1838, after four years of unpaid 'apprenticeship'.

toll.money: £20 million, about 40% of the Treasury's annual budget, was borrowed in 1835 to compensate slave-owners. The loan was only finally paid off by the taxpayer in 2015. The people who had been enslaved received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The £20 million figure and the 2015 repayment date are from HM Treasury and the Legacies of British Slavery database at University College London.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.supports: £20 million, about 40% of the Treasury's annual budget, was borrowed in 1835 to compensate slave-owners.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

commonwealth.note: The London Declaration of 28 April 1949 let India stay in as a republic and turned a club of settler dominions into an association of 56 states, some of which Britain never ruled.

consequences.economicLegacy: Empire concentrated its profits: the City, shipping, insurance and the great trading houses gained most, while defence costs fell on all taxpayers and cheap sugar, tea, cotton and grain reached working-class tables.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, the Westminster parliamentary model and the English language went out with the empire and stayed after it, which is why a third of the world's people now live in states using one or more of the three.

peak.populationNote: 2021 census for England, Wales and Scotland combined. In 1801, when the empire was already large, Great Britain held about 10.5 million people.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Great Britain’s largest recorded population: 65,077,200 people, counted in 2021.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Great Britain’s greatest extent, 228,550 km² in 2021: the 3 map units this atlas draws it holding that year measure 228,550 km², the same figure.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Linda Colley
evidence.work: Britons: Forging the Nation 1707-1837
evidence.supports: How a British national identity was assembled after 1707, and the place of empire and war in making it.

evidence.author: T. M. Devine
evidence.work: Scotland's Empire, 1600-1815
evidence.supports: Darien, the Union bargain, and the Scottish share in imperial trade, administration and settlement.

evidence.author: John Darwin
evidence.work: The Empire Project: The Rise and Fall of the British World-System, 1830-1970
evidence.supports: How a medium-sized European state sustained a global system, and what it cost.

contested.note: Historians disagree sharply about whether empire enriched Britain as a whole or transferred money from taxpayers to investors, and about whether ordinary Britons noticed the empire at all — compare Bernard Porter's argument in 'The Absent-Minded Imperialists' with Catherine Hall and Sonya Rose's 'At Home with the Empire'.

pedagogy.hook: The state that came to rule a quarter of the world was itself only made in 1707, and it was assembled by conquest in Wales and a bought treaty in Scotland.

misconception.belief: Britain is an ancient country that went out and built an empire.
misconception.correction: The Kingdom of Great Britain was created on 1 May 1707, eighty years after Barbados and a century after Jamestown. Wales had been conquered by Edward I in 1282-83 and annexed by statute in 1536; Scotland's parliament dissolved itself in 1707 after its own colony at Darien failed. The nation and the empire were built together.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Empire was not something a finished Britain did to the world. The Union, the navy, the national debt and the empire grew out of one another, and Scots, Welsh and Irish people were both governed by this state and among its most effective agents abroad.

keyDates.what: Statute of Rhuddlan: Wales under English law
Laws in Wales Acts annex Wales to England
Union with Scotland creates Great Britain
Union with Ireland creates the United Kingdom
Statute of Westminster: the dominions become independent
Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly open

territories.name: Ireland
territories.formalName: The Kingdom of Ireland, then part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

namesOverTime.name: Lordship of Ireland
namesOverTime.note: The Anglo-Norman lordship held the Pale around Dublin and scattered lordships; most of the island lived under Gaelic law, which the English called no law at all.

namesOverTime.name: Eire
namesOverTime.note: The 1937 constitution named the state Eire, or in the English language Ireland, and claimed the whole island until that claim was removed by referendum in 1998.

namesOverTime.name: Northern Ireland
namesOverTime.note: Six of Ulster's nine counties. Irish nationalists more often say 'the north of Ireland' or 'the six counties'; what you call it signals what you think of it.

modernSuccessors.name: Ireland
modernSuccessors.note: A dominion called the Irish Free State from 1922, renamed Eire under a new constitution in 1937, and a republic outside the Commonwealth from 18 April 1949.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: In 1541 the claim covered the whole island but the reality did not: outside the Pale, English law reached only as far as an army could march. It is drawn partial until the surrender at Mellifont in 1603.

geoCoverage.label: Northern Ireland only
geoCoverage.change: The 26 southern counties leave as the Irish Free State. Six of Ulster's nine counties stay in the United Kingdom, and are still in it.

acquisitions.how: The Irish Parliament, packed and managed from Dublin Castle, declared Henry VIII King of Ireland, upgrading a 370-year-old lordship into a kingdom he did not yet control.

counterparties.name: Gaelic Irish lordships
counterparties.lost: Recognition as independent rulers. Under 'surrender and regrant' they had to hand their lands to the king and receive them back as English-style earls, holding by English inheritance law instead of Gaelic election.

counterparties.name: Hiberno-Norman lords
counterparties.lost: Their semi-independence, above all the Fitzgeralds of Kildare, whose rebellion of 1534-35 was destroyed and whose lands were confiscated.

instrument.name: Crown of Ireland Act
instrument.note: Passed by the Irish Parliament in June 1541; the corresponding English statute is conventionally dated 1542.

acquisitions.how: Hugh O'Neill surrendered at Mellifont after nine years of war, a Spanish landing and a campaign that deliberately burned Ulster's harvests; for the first time English law ran over the whole island.

counterparties.name: Gaelic lordships of Ulster
counterparties.lost: Independence, and then their land: after the Flight of the Earls in September 1607 their estates were confiscated and planted with English and Scottish settlers under a scheme drafted in London.

people.name: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone
people.role: led the confederacy of Gaelic lords for nine years

people.name: Red Hugh O'Donnell
people.role: lord of Tyrconnell; escaped from Dublin Castle to lead the western war and died in Spain seeking help

people.name: Charles Blount, Lord Mountjoy
people.role: commanded the English campaign of famine and fort-building that ended the war

cost.note: Most deaths came from the deliberate destruction of harvests in Ulster in 1601-02. The surviving accounts are English and partisan, which is why the range is so wide.

warrant.author: The English commanders and administrators in Ireland, in the surviving accounts
warrant.work: English accounts of the Nine Years War and the wasting of Ulster
warrant.supports: Most deaths came from the deliberate destruction of harvests in Ulster in 1601-02. The surviving accounts are English and partisan, which is why the range is so wide.
warrant.check: Calendar of State Papers, Ireland, 1600–03; and the Carew manuscripts at Lambeth Palace Library.
warrant.note: The record says these accounts are English and partisan. The width of the range is what that partisanship looks like once it is turned into a number.

acquisitions.resistance: Nine years of war, ending with the defeat of a joint Irish and Spanish force outside Kinsale on 24 December 1601 after a 500-kilometre winter march.

acquisitions.how: Cromwell's reconquest ended with the Act for the Settlement of Ireland, which confiscated the land of Catholic landowners east of the Shannon and ordered them to Connacht to take poorer land or none.

counterparties.name: Confederate Catholic Ireland
counterparties.lost: Almost everything: Catholic ownership of Irish land fell from roughly 60% in 1641 to under 10% by 1660, and the confiscated estates paid the soldiers and the London investors who had funded the war.

instrument.name: Act for the Settlement of Ireland

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: commanded the reconquest of 1649-50 and ordered the storms of Drogheda and Wexford

people.name: Owen Roe O'Neill
people.role: commanded the Confederate Ulster army; won at Benburb in 1646 and died in 1649

cost.note: Deaths across the wars of 1641-53 from fighting, famine and plague. William Petty's contemporary figure of 616,000 is disputed; modern estimates put the population loss between 15% and 40%.

warrant.author: Sir William Petty, against modern population-loss reconstructions
warrant.supports: Deaths across the wars of 1641-53 from fighting, famine and plague. William Petty's contemporary figure of 616,000 is disputed; modern estimates put the population loss between 15% and 40%.
warrant.check: Petty, The Political Anatomy of Ireland (London, 1691). The modern range is reconstructed from the 1659 census, the Down Survey and the hearth-money returns.
warrant.note: Petty surveyed the confiscated land himself and was paid in it. His 616,000 is disputed; the atlas prints the dispute rather than choosing a side of it.

contested.note: The scale of mortality, and whether the storms of Drogheda and Wexford were within the laws of war of the time, are both actively argued. So is the number of Irish people shipped to the Caribbean as indentured labour, which is often exaggerated online into a myth of 'Irish slaves'.

acquisitions.how: The Treaty of Limerick ended the Jacobite war on terms promising Catholics the toleration they had had under Charles II; the Irish Parliament broke those terms within five years with the Penal Laws.

counterparties.name: Jacobite Ireland
counterparties.lost: The last Catholic army in Ireland. About 14,000 soldiers sailed for France in the 'Flight of the Wild Geese', and Catholics were then barred from parliament, the bar, the army, and from buying land.

people.name: Patrick Sarsfield, Earl of Lucan
people.role: led the Jacobite defence of Limerick and negotiated the treaty, then left for France

people.name: Godert de Ginkel
people.role: Williamite commander who signed the treaty at Limerick

statusPeriods.label: Kingdom of Ireland under Poynings' Law
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ireland had its own parliament in Dublin, but under Poynings' Law of 1494 it could not meet or pass a bill without London's approval, and after 1691 only Protestants could sit in it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Dublin Castle, under the English and then British government
statusPeriods.franchise: Catholics, about three quarters of the population, could not sit in parliament from 1691 and could not vote at all between 1728 and 1793.
statusPeriods.note: Formally a kingdom in personal union with England, not a colony. Historians argue about the label; the atlas uses 'representative-colony' for how power actually worked and says so here. Grattan's Parliament won legislative independence in 1782; it lasted eighteen years.

statusPeriods.label: Part of the United Kingdom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Dublin parliament voted itself out of existence and Ireland sent about 100 MPs to Westminster, where they were always outnumbered; the country was still run day to day by a Lord Lieutenant and a Chief Secretary in Dublin Castle.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Westminster and Dublin Castle
statusPeriods.franchise: Catholic Emancipation in 1829 let Catholics sit at Westminster; the property franchise kept most Irish men and all women off the register until 1918.
statusPeriods.note: Ireland was legally part of the United Kingdom throughout the Great Famine of 1845-52, which killed about a million of its citizens while food was exported under military escort. Coercion acts suspending ordinary law were passed for Ireland dozens of times in this century.

statusPeriods.label: Northern Ireland remains in the United Kingdom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Six counties keep a devolved parliament at Stormont, run continuously by the Ulster Unionist Party from 1921 to 1972, then are ruled directly from London through thirty years of conflict, then devolved again under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Belfast and Westminster
statusPeriods.franchise: Stormont kept a property qualification in local elections until 1969 and drew ward boundaries that gave unionist minorities control of nationalist towns such as Derry; the civil rights movement of 1968 demanded 'one man, one vote'.
statusPeriods.note: The same status continues, but the extent changes: that is why a new status period begins here.

departures.how: Two and a half years of guerrilla war ended in a truce, then a treaty that gave 26 counties dominion status inside the empire and kept six in the United Kingdom; the men who signed it then fought each other over it.

led.name: Michael Collins
led.role: director of intelligence of the IRA, signed the Treaty, killed in the Civil War ten months later

led.name: Arthur Griffith
led.role: founder of Sinn Fein, led the treaty delegation

led.name: Eamon de Valera
led.role: president of the Dail who rejected the Treaty and led the losing side in the Civil War, then governed the state for most of the next forty years

led.name: Constance Markievicz
led.role: fought in 1916, first woman elected to the House of Commons, refused the Treaty

led.name: David Lloyd George
led.role: Prime Minister who threatened 'immediate and terrible war' to get the Treaty signed

led.name: James Craig
led.role: first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland

departures.movement: Sinn Fein and the Irish Republican Army

cost.note: About 1,400 died in the War of Independence to July 1921 and between 1,000 and 3,000 in the Civil War of 1922-23, where the counting is worst. Figures follow Charles Townshend and Michael Hopkinson.

warrant.author: Charles Townshend
warrant.work: The Republic: The Fight for Irish Independence, 1918-1923
warrant.supports: The war, the Treaty negotiations and the casualty figures.

departures.borders: The border was drawn around six of Ulster's nine counties, chosen because that was the largest area with a secure unionist majority; a Boundary Commission was promised in 1921, reported in 1925, and was shelved unpublished.

instrument.name: Anglo-Irish Treaty
instrument.note: Signed on 6 December 1921 and in force exactly one year later, when the Irish Free State came into existence.

contested.note: Whether the Treaty was the most that could be got or a surrender is still the fault line of Irish politics: the two largest parties in the Republic descend from the two sides of the split.

evidence.author: Charles Townshend
evidence.work: The Republic: The Fight for Irish Independence, 1918-1923
evidence.supports: The war, the Treaty negotiations and the casualty figures.

stillBritish.note: Northern Ireland, six counties and about 1.9 million people, is still part of the United Kingdom; the 1998 Good Friday Agreement says it stays until majorities on either side of the border vote otherwise.

partition.note: Partition created a state with a permanent unionist majority and a large nationalist minority, and thirty years of conflict from 1968 killed about 3,500 people.
partition.lineDrawnBy: the Government of Ireland Act 1920, drawn around six counties rather than the historic nine of Ulster because nine would not have held a unionist majority

violence.note: Conquest, plantation, penal law, famine, insurrection and a thirty-year conflict after partition: Ireland is where nearly every technique of British rule was tried first, and where several were tried last.

populationTransfer.note: The Great Famine of 1845-52 killed about a million people and drove another million abroad; Ireland's population is still below its 1841 level, the only country in Europe of which that is true.

toll.note: Excess deaths 1846-51 as estimated by Cormac O Grada and by Joel Mokyr; emigration figures from passenger records, which undercount.

warrant.author: Cormac O Grada
warrant.work: Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory
warrant.supports: Excess deaths 1846-51 as estimated by Cormac O Grada and by Joel Mokyr; emigration figures from passenger records, which undercount.
warrant.check: Princeton University Press, 1999. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

commonwealth.note: The Republic of Ireland Act came into force on Easter Monday 1949 and put Ireland outside the Commonwealth: leaving the empire in 1922 and leaving the Commonwealth in 1949 are two different events, twenty-seven years apart.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain also kept three naval bases in the Free State — Berehaven, Cobh and Lough Swilly, the 'Treaty Ports' — until Neville Chamberlain handed them back in 1938, which let Ireland stay neutral in the Second World War.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 499-kilometre border drawn in 1921 became the European Union's only land frontier with the United Kingdom in 2020, and dominated the Brexit negotiations for four years.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Irish was spoken by roughly half the population in 1800 and by a small minority a century later; English common law, the land registry and a national police force are all inheritances of the union.

peak.populationNote: The 1841 census, taken four years before the famine. The island has never again held that many people; the combined figure today is about 7.1 million.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Ireland’s largest recorded population: 8,175,124 people, counted in 1841.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: R. F. Foster
evidence.work: Modern Ireland 1600-1972
evidence.supports: The long narrative from plantation to partition.

evidence.author: Nicholas Canny
evidence.work: Making Ireland British, 1580-1650
evidence.supports: Plantation policy and its export to the Atlantic colonies.

evidence.author: Cormac O Grada
evidence.work: Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory
evidence.supports: Famine mortality and emigration estimates.

contested.note: Whether Ireland was a colony at all is a live argument: it sent MPs to Westminster and Irish people governed and soldiered across the empire, yet it was conquered, planted, and governed under emergency law for much of the nineteenth century. The atlas shows both facts rather than choosing between them.

pedagogy.hook: The plantation methods tried on Munster in the 1580s were carried to Virginia in the 1600s by some of the same men, including Walter Raleigh.

misconception.belief: Ireland was a foreign country that Britain invaded, and independence came in 1916.
misconception.correction: From 1801 to 1922 Ireland was legally part of the United Kingdom, sending about 100 MPs to Westminster. The Easter Rising of 1916 failed in six days and was unpopular in Dublin; what changed everything was the execution of fifteen of its leaders over nine days in May. Independence came in 1922, and only for 26 of the 32 counties.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Ireland is the empire's first laboratory and its longest unfinished business: plantation, indirect rule, coercion acts and partition were all tried here before they were exported, and the border drawn in 1921 is still the hardest problem in British politics.

territories.name: Isle of Man
territories.formalName: The Isle of Man (Ellan Vannin), a Crown dependency

namesOverTime.name: Kingdom of Mann and the Isles

from.note: Godred Crovan's conquest is the conventional start; the Norse-Gaelic kingdom's early dates are uncertain.

namesOverTime.note: Norway sold Mann and the Hebrides to Scotland at the Treaty of Perth for 4,000 marks and 100 marks a year.

namesOverTime.name: Lordship of Mann
namesOverTime.note: Held as private property by the Stanley earls of Derby from 1405 and by the Murray dukes of Atholl from 1736.

namesOverTime.name: Isle of Man / Ellan Vannin
namesOverTime.note: A Crown dependency, not part of the United Kingdom: Tynwald legislates for it and Westminster does not, though the UK runs its defence and foreign relations.

modernSuccessors.name: Isle of Man
modernSuccessors.note: Not a country in the United Nations sense: a self-governing Crown dependency whose defence and foreign relations are Britain's responsibility.

from.note: English control was intermittent for a generation after 1333; the island changed hands several times before the Stanley grant of 1405.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: A 572-square-kilometre island in the middle of the Irish Sea, in sight of England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales on a clear day.

acquisitions.how: William Montagu, a favourite of Edward III, took Mann from its Scottish garrison and had himself styled King of Mann; English kings then handed the island on as private property, to the Stanleys from 1405 and the Murrays from 1736.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Scotland
counterparties.lost: An island Norway had sold to Scotland in 1266 under the Treaty of Perth, and which Scotland had held for less than seventy years.

counterparties.name: The Manx
counterparties.lost: Any say in who owned them. From 1333 the island was a piece of property that English kings granted to favourites, and its people came with it.
counterparties.note: Tynwald, the island's assembly, kept meeting throughout and still does; the Manx kept their law even when they did not keep their lord.

people.name: William Montagu, 1st Earl of Salisbury
people.role: seized the island in 1333 and styled himself King of Mann

contested.note: Control between 1290 and 1405 flipped repeatedly between Scottish and English claimants and the dates given by different chroniclers do not agree. What is not disputed is that after 1405 the island was English-held property.

acquisitions.how: Parliament bought the lordship of Mann from John Murray, 3rd Duke of Atholl, and his wife Charlotte for £70,000, purely to shut down the duty-free harbours through which tea, brandy, rum and tobacco were being run into Britain and Ireland.

counterparties.name: The Dukes of Atholl
counterparties.lost: The lordship of an island, for £70,000 and an annuity — a price they spent the next sixty years complaining about, and got topped up in 1828.

counterparties.name: The Manx
counterparties.lost: Their economy. The 'running trade' had made Douglas and Peel prosperous; British customs officers arrived, the trade died, and the island stayed poor for two generations.
counterparties.note: Manx people still call 1765 'the Revestment'. Nobody asked them, and Tynwald was not consulted.

instrument.name: Isle of Man Purchase Act 1765 (the Revestment Act)
instrument.note: It revested the lordship in the Crown; the Atholls kept their manorial rights and patronage until a second purchase in 1828 for £417,144.

statusPeriods.label: A private lordship of the Stanleys and the Murrays
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Lord of Mann appointed the Governor and took the island's revenues; Tynwald met on the open-air mound at St John's and made Manx law, and English kings interfered only when they wanted something.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Castle Rushen, under a lord resident in England
statusPeriods.franchise: The House of Keys was self-electing: its 24 members chose their own replacements, and did so until 1866.
statusPeriods.note: Tynwald claims descent from a Norse assembly of about 979 and calls itself the oldest continuous parliament in the world; the claim rests on continuity of the institution, not of unbroken records.

statusPeriods.label: Crown dependency: not a colony, and not part of the UK
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown holds the Lordship of Mann. Tynwald makes the island's laws and sets its taxes; the United Kingdom is responsible for defence and foreign relations and does not legislate for the island without its consent.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Douglas, with a Lieutenant Governor appointed by the Crown
statusPeriods.franchise: Manx women who owned property could vote for the House of Keys from 1881, the first national parliamentary franchise for women anywhere; all adults from 1919, and sixteen-year-olds since 2006.
statusPeriods.note: The Keys became popularly elected in 1866. Real self-government came slowly: the Lieutenant Governor still controlled the island's finances until 1958, and the first Manx Chief Minister took office in 1986.

departures.how: The Isle of Man has never left, because it never joined: it is a possession of the Crown that has never been part of the United Kingdom, sends no MPs to Westminster, and was not in the European Union even when Britain was.

stillBritish.note: A self-governing Crown dependency of about 84,000 people; Tynwald legislates, the Crown appoints a Lieutenant Governor, and the United Kingdom handles defence and foreign affairs.

violence.note: The island became Britain's internment camp twice: about 23,000 civilians of enemy nationality were held at Knockaloe near Peel in the First World War, and thousands more, most of them refugees from Nazism, in the Second.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Revestment killed the smuggling trade that had built Douglas; Victorian tourism from Lancashire replaced it, and offshore banking and low taxes replaced that after the 1960s.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Manx Gaelic's last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974; the language is now taught in a Manx-medium primary school and spoken by a few thousand learners. Manx law is its own, and Acts of Tynwald are still promulgated aloud in Manx and English every 5 July.

peak.populationNote: 2021 Isle of Man census. The population was about 52,000 in 1851, fell with emigration, and passed 80,000 only in the 2000s.

pedagogy.hook: Britain did not conquer the Isle of Man in 1765. It bought it, for £70,000, to stop the Manx smuggling tea.

misconception.belief: The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are part of the United Kingdom, or were British colonies.
misconception.correction: They are Crown dependencies: possessions of the Crown that have never been part of the UK and were never governed by the Colonial Office. They send no MPs to Westminster, set their own taxes, and make their own laws through Tynwald and the States. That is why they could stay outside the EU while Britain was in it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The crown dependencies prove that 'British' was never one legal category. Three islands within sight of Britain have a constitutional status shared with nowhere else in the empire, and it is the reason they became offshore financial centres.

territories.name: Jersey
territories.formalName: The Bailiwick of Jersey, a Crown dependency

namesOverTime.name: Bailiwick of Jersey
namesOverTime.note: The island's own Norman French speech, Jerriais, was the everyday language into the twentieth century and is still taught in schools.

modernSuccessors.name: Jersey
modernSuccessors.note: Self-governing, but not a sovereign state: the United Kingdom is responsible for its defence and represents it abroad.

geoCoverage.label: The island and its reefs
geoCoverage.change: Jersey lies 22 kilometres from France and 160 from England, which is the whole of its history in one measurement.

acquisitions.how: When Philip II of France took Normandy from King John in 1204, Jersey stayed with John because he was still its Duke; England kept the island not by taking it but by not losing it, and it has never been part of England since.

counterparties.name: The Duchy of Normandy and the Kings of France
counterparties.lost: The last fragment of Normandy. France invaded the islands in 1338-45, held Mont Orgueil from 1461 to 1468, and landed at St Helier as late as January 1781, and never got them back.
counterparties.note: No British category fits this. Jersey was not conquered, settled, ceded or bought: it is the remnant of a duchy, and the model records it as an annexation only because there is no better term.

counterparties.name: The islanders of Jersey, under Norman customary law
counterparties.lost: Nothing, in 1204. Jersey kept the Coutume de Normandie, and still keeps it: the island's law is the customary law of a duchy that has not existed in France for eight hundred years.
counterparties.note: The Clameur de Haro - a cry of 'Haro, haro, a l'aide mon Prince, on me fait tort' that halts a wrong on the spot - is still pleadable in a Jersey court. Jerriais, the island's Norman French, is spoken by a few hundred people and taught in schools.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris (1259)
instrument.note: Henry III renounced his claim to Normandy but kept the islands, which is the nearest thing to a legal title Jersey's British status has.

people.name: King John
people.role: lost Normandy in 1204 and kept the islands

people.name: Francis Peirson
people.role: 24-year-old major who led the British and Jersey militia counter-attack in the Battle of Jersey on 6 January 1781, and was killed in the Royal Square

acquisitions.resistance: Jersey defended itself against France repeatedly with its own militia; the last invasion, in January 1781, was beaten in a morning in the square in front of the market house in St Helier.

statusPeriods.label: Possession of the Crown, governed by its own States
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown appoints a Lieutenant Governor and the Bailiff who presides over both the court and the assembly; the States of Jersey make the island's law, and Westminster legislates for Jersey only by convention with its agreement.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Helier, with a Lieutenant Governor and a Bailiff appointed by the Crown
statusPeriods.franchise: The States were dominated by the twelve parish rectors and the jurats until reform in 1948; elected deputies were added in 1857 and women could vote from 1919.
statusPeriods.note: The term 'Crown dependency' is modern; the relationship is medieval and has never been written down in one document. Jersey still uses the Clameur de Haro, a shouted appeal to Duke Rollo of Normandy, as a legally effective way to stop work on disputed land.

statusPeriods.label: Under German occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: German forces landed on 1 July 1940 after Britain demilitarised and evacuated what it could; the Bailiff and the States stayed and administered the island under German orders for five years, which is what makes the occupation so hard to judge.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was nil: the islands were the only British territory in Europe occupied by Nazi Germany. Degree 0 records the loss of control, not its strength.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Helier, under the German Feldkommandantur 515 in Guernsey
statusPeriods.note: Some 1,200 people were deported from Jersey to internment camps in Germany in September 1942 and February 1943 for being born in Britain. Twenty-two Jersey people died in Nazi camps on the continent.

statusPeriods.label: Crown dependency and offshore finance centre
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The States of Jersey were reformed in 1948, the rectors and jurats lost their seats, and the island has since run its own tax system; a ministerial government replaced committee rule in 2005.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Helier
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; sixteen-year-olds have voted since 2008.

departures.how: Jersey has not left and cannot straightforwardly leave: it is not part of the United Kingdom, was never a colony, and has no independence movement of any size, though it has taken over more of its own affairs decade by decade.

stillBritish.note: Jersey is a self-governing Crown dependency of about 103,000 people, with its own parliament, taxes, courts and immigration rules, and no representation at Westminster.

violence.note: In September 1942 and February 1943 about 1,200 Jersey residents born in Britain were deported to camps in Germany on Hitler's personal order; 22 islanders died in Nazi camps, and the winter of 1944-45 brought the island close to starvation.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cider, potatoes and Jersey cattle gave way after 1960 to banking and trusts: financial services now provide about two fifths of the island's economy, and Jersey's tax status has been a standing argument with Westminster and Brussels ever since.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Jersey's law is still partly the customary law of Normandy, its property registry works in French, and until the 1900s the States debated in French. The Clameur de Haro, an appeal to a tenth-century Norman duke, remains legally valid.

peak.populationNote: 2021 Jersey census. About 10,000 islanders were evacuated to England in June 1940 and roughly 41,000 stayed for the occupation.

evidence.author: John Le Patourel
evidence.work: The Medieval Administration of the Channel Islands, 1199-1399
evidence.supports: How the islands stayed with the English Crown after the loss of Normandy, and how their separate law survived.

evidence.author: Paul Sanders
evidence.work: The British Channel Islands under German Occupation, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The occupation, the deportations, and the conduct of the island administrations.

evidence.author: Madeleine Bunting
evidence.work: The Model Occupation: The Channel Islands under German Rule, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The argument about collaboration and accommodation on the islands, and the postwar silence about it.

contested.note: How far the island authorities collaborated with the German administration has been argued since Madeleine Bunting's book in 1995. Defenders point out that an unarmed, undefended civilian population had no alternative; critics point to the registration of Jews and the enforcement of German orders by island police.

pedagogy.hook: Jersey has belonged to the English Crown since 1204 — not because England took it, but because it refused to go with Normandy when Normandy went to France.

misconception.belief: Britain was never occupied in the Second World War.
misconception.correction: The Channel Islands were occupied from 30 June 1940 to 9 May 1945. Britain decided the islands could not be defended, demilitarised them without telling the Germans, and evacuated about a quarter of the population. Some 1,200 Jersey residents were later deported to camps in Germany.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Jersey is the oldest possession of the English Crown and one of the newest kinds of economy, and it is the one place where British civilians lived for five years under Nazi rule, administered by their own officials.

territories.name: Guernsey
territories.formalName: The Bailiwick of Guernsey, a Crown dependency, including Alderney, Sark and Herm

modernSuccessors.name: Guernsey
modernSuccessors.note: The Bailiwick includes Alderney and Sark, which have their own parliaments — Sark's was a feudal court until 2008, when it held its first general election.

geoCoverage.label: Guernsey, Alderney, Sark and Herm
geoCoverage.change: Three inhabited islands and a scatter of smaller ones, closer to France than to England, held together as one bailiwick since the thirteenth century.

acquisitions.how: Guernsey, like Jersey, stayed with King John when he lost Normandy in 1204, and was governed thereafter as a separate bailiwick answering directly to the Crown rather than to any English county or court.

counterparties.name: The Duchy of Normandy and the Kings of France
counterparties.lost: The islands off their own coast. France raided and briefly held parts of the bailiwick several times in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries but never kept them.
counterparties.note: In 1483 a papal bull declared the islands neutral in Anglo-French wars, and the privilege was respected for three centuries.

counterparties.name: The islanders of Guernsey, under Norman customary law
counterparties.lost: Nothing, in 1204. Guernsey kept Norman customary law and its own courts, and answered to the Crown rather than to any English county or bishop.
counterparties.note: Guernesiais, the island's Norman French, is still spoken by a small number of mostly older islanders. The Royal Court of Guernsey traces its jurisdiction to the loss of Normandy, not to a grant from England.

statusPeriods.label: Bailiwick of the Crown with its own States
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown appoints a Lieutenant Governor and a Bailiff; the States of Deliberation legislate for Guernsey, Alderney has its own States and Sark had a feudal Chief Pleas presided over by a Seigneur until 2008.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Peter Port, with a Crown-appointed Lieutenant Governor and Bailiff
statusPeriods.franchise: Rectors and jurats sat in the States by right until 1948; women could vote from 1921, and Sark's parliament was made fully elected only in 2008 after a European Court of Human Rights case.

statusPeriods.label: Under German occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: German aircraft bombed St Peter Port's harbour on 28 June 1940, killing 34 people, not knowing the islands had been demilitarised; troops landed on 30 June and ran the bailiwick through the existing States and police for five years.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was nil. Degree 0 records occupation by another power, as the model specifies, not the strength of British control.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Peter Port, under Feldkommandantur 515
statusPeriods.note: Alderney was evacuated almost completely and became a labour island: the Germans built four camps there, one of which, Lager Sylt, was run by the SS from March 1943 as a subcamp of Neuengamme.

statusPeriods.label: Crown dependency and finance centre
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The States were reformed in 1948, the island rebuilt its tomato and then its finance industry, and Guernsey now sets its own taxes and immigration rules while Britain handles defence and diplomacy.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Peter Port
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; Guernsey elects its deputies without political parties, in island-wide voting since 2020.

departures.how: Guernsey remains a Crown dependency: never part of the United Kingdom, never administered by the Colonial Office, and outside the European Union even during Britain's membership.

stillBritish.note: The Bailiwick of Guernsey is self-governing, with about 64,000 people in Guernsey, Alderney, Sark and Herm; Britain is responsible only for its defence and its representation abroad.

violence.note: On Alderney the Germans ran four labour camps, one of them an SS concentration camp; a 2024 British government review put the number of people who died there at between 641 and 1,027, most of them Soviet and eastern European forced labourers.

toll.note: The range is the finding of the expert review commissioned by the UK government and published in 2024, which examined earlier claims of far higher totals and did not sustain them.

populationTransfer.note: Alderney's entire civilian population of about 1,500 was evacuated to Britain in June 1940 and could not return until December 1945; Guernsey sent about 5,000 children away with their schools.

consequences.economicLegacy: Granite quarrying and then greenhouse tomatoes carried the island until the 1970s; insurance, funds and banking replaced them, and Guernsey has fought the same arguments about tax transparency as Jersey.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Guernesiais, the island's Norman French, has a few hundred speakers left. The law is Norman customary law overlaid with island statute, and the Bailiff still presides over both the court and the parliament.

peak.populationNote: About 64,000 people live in the Bailiwick: roughly 63,000 in Guernsey, some 2,000 on Alderney and about 500 on Sark. These are States of Guernsey estimates rather than a full census.

evidence.author: Paul Sanders
evidence.work: The British Channel Islands under German Occupation, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The occupation administration, the registration and deportation of Jewish residents, and the Alderney camps.

evidence.author: Madeleine Bunting
evidence.work: The Model Occupation: The Channel Islands under German Rule, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The postwar argument about collaboration and about what the islands' authorities knew.

contested.note: The number of people who died on Alderney has been claimed as anything from a few hundred to tens of thousands. A review commissioned by the UK government and published in 2024 concluded that between 641 and 1,027 people died there. The figures before that review were poorly sourced, and this record uses the review's range.

pedagogy.hook: The only Nazi concentration camp on British soil was on Alderney in the Channel Islands, run by the SS from March 1943.

misconception.belief: Nothing that happened in the Holocaust touched British territory or British officials.
misconception.correction: Guernsey's own administration registered the islands' Jewish residents under German orders in 1940. Three Jewish women living in Guernsey — Therese Steiner, Auguste Spitz and Marianne Grunfeld — were deported in April 1942 and murdered at Auschwitz. On Alderney the SS ran a camp in which hundreds of forced labourers died.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Guernsey is where the question every occupied country in Europe faced — what do you do when the orders come from an occupier and you are the local official? — was faced by British officials on British soil.

territories.name: Gibraltar
territories.formalName: The City and Garrison of Gibraltar, a British Overseas Territory

namesOverTime.name: Jabal Tariq

from.note: Tariq ibn Ziyad landed in 711; the year is given as a four-digit value here only because the data format requires it.

namesOverTime.note: 'Tariq's mountain', after Tariq ibn Ziyad, who landed there in 711. Gibraltar is a Spanish corruption of the Arabic name; the rock was Muslim-ruled for about 750 years, Spanish for 242 and British for over 320.

modernSuccessors.name: Gibraltar (United Kingdom)
modernSuccessors.note: Claimed by Spain, which has never accepted the 1967 and 2002 referendums; the United Nations still lists Gibraltar as a non-self-governing territory.

geoCoverage.label: The Rock and the town
geoCoverage.change: Six and a half square kilometres: a limestone ridge, a town at its foot, and an airstrip built across the isthmus in the 1940s on ground Spain says was never ceded.

acquisitions.how: An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Sir George Rooke bombarded Gibraltar for five hours and stormed it in three days during the War of the Spanish Succession, claiming it not for Britain but for the Habsburg claimant to the Spanish throne, Archduke Charles.

counterparties.name: The town of Gibraltar and the Spanish Crown
counterparties.lost: The rock, the harbour and the town. Almost all of the roughly 4,000 residents left within days, taking the town records and the statue of Our Lady of Europe, and founded San Roque, which still calls itself 'Gibraltar in exile'.
counterparties.note: The population left partly in loyalty to Philip V and partly because the storming was followed by looting and by attacks on the town's churches.

people.name: Sir George Rooke
people.role: commanded the Anglo-Dutch fleet that took the Rock

people.name: Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt
people.role: commanded the landing force and governed in the Habsburg claimant's name; killed defending Gibraltar in 1705

people.name: Diego de Salinas
people.role: Spanish governor who surrendered with a garrison of about 150 men and led the townspeople out to San Roque

acquisitions.resistance: Spain besieged Gibraltar in 1704-05, in 1727, and for three years and seven months from 1779 to 1783 — the Great Siege, the longest siege in British military history.

acquisitions.how: Spain ceded 'the town and castle of Gibraltar, together with the port, fortifications and forts thereunto belonging' to Britain for ever, with no territorial jurisdiction, no open communication by land, and a promise that Spain would get first refusal if Britain ever gave it up.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Spain
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over the Rock, and the Balearic island of Minorca in the next article of the same treaty; Spain has demanded Gibraltar back at intervals ever since and has never stopped.
counterparties.note: Article X of the Treaty of Utrecht is still the legal basis of the dispute, and Britain and Spain each quote it: Britain for the cession, Spain for the limits on it.

instrument.name: Treaty of Utrecht, Article X
instrument.note: The Anglo-Spanish treaty of Utrecht. Article X also barred Jews and Muslims from living in Gibraltar, a clause Britain ignored almost at once: Sephardic Jewish and Genoese families were among the town's founders.

statusPeriods.label: Held by force, in another king's name
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For nine years Gibraltar was garrisoned by British troops but claimed for the Habsburg candidate to the Spanish throne; the British commander governed and the legal title belonged to nobody in particular.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The garrison, under the fleet

statusPeriods.label: A fortress run by its garrison
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Governor was always a general and the Rock was a naval base with a town attached: civilians needed permits to live there, the dockyard was the employer, and Gibraltar had no elected legislature at all until 1950.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Convent, Gibraltar, under the War Office and later the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: None until a City Council was elected in 1921, and no elected legislature until 1950. In 1940 the entire civilian population, about 13,000 people, was evacuated to Britain, Madeira and Jamaica; some were not allowed home until 1951.
statusPeriods.note: Gibraltar was formally constituted a Crown Colony only in 1830; before that it was governed simply as a garrison. The status is dated from the cession because that is when British sovereignty began.

statusPeriods.label: Self-governing British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1969 constitution gave Gibraltar an elected House of Assembly and a Chief Minister running everything but defence, foreign affairs and internal security; a new constitution in 2006 went further. Spain closed the land frontier nine days after the 1969 constitution and kept it shut for sixteen years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Gibraltar, with a UK-appointed Governor
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage. Gibraltarians voted in UK European Parliament elections from 2004 and voted 96% to remain in the EU in 2016, and left anyway.

departures.how: Gibraltar has not left, and has twice voted overwhelmingly not to: 12,138 to 44 against Spanish sovereignty in 1967, and 17,900 to 187 against sharing sovereignty with Spain in 2002.

stillBritish.note: About 32,000 people live on six and a half square kilometres of British sovereign territory attached to Spain, which claims it; the United Nations still lists Gibraltar as awaiting decolonisation.

populationTransfer.note: The Spanish population left in 1704 and was replaced by Genoese, Portuguese, Menorcan, Maltese, Sephardic Jewish and Moroccan incomers; in 1940 the whole civilian population was evacuated for the war, and thousands were kept out for years afterwards.

consequences.borderLegacy: Spain closed the land frontier completely from 1969 to 1982 and fully reopened it only in 1985; after Brexit Gibraltar was left outside both the EU and the UK's trade deal, and its border arrangements were still being negotiated years later.
consequences.economicLegacy: The dockyard and the garrison were the economy until Britain ran them down in the 1980s; online gambling, shipping services and financial services replaced them, and about 15,000 workers now cross the frontier from Spain each day.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Gibraltarians speak llanito, a Spanish-English mix with Genoese and Hebrew words in it, and English law applies with a Gibraltar Parliament to amend it.

peak.populationNote: Government of Gibraltar estimate. The garrison sometimes outnumbered the civilians: during the Great Siege of 1779-83 about 7,500 soldiers held the Rock.

evidence.author: Chris Grocott and Gareth Stockey
evidence.work: Gibraltar: A Modern History
evidence.supports: The twentieth-century politics of the Rock: evacuation, the frontier closure, and the referendums.

evidence.author: Stephen Constantine
evidence.work: Community and Identity: The Making of Modern Gibraltar since 1704
evidence.supports: How the population that left in 1704 was replaced, and how Gibraltarian identity formed.

contested.note: Britain and Spain read the same treaty article differently. Britain says Article X of Utrecht ceded Gibraltar outright; Spain says the cession was of the town, castle and port only, that the isthmus where the airport stands was never included, and that the Gibraltarians are a transplanted population whose votes cannot settle a territorial question.

pedagogy.hook: Britain captured Gibraltar in 1704 in the name of a Spanish king — and then kept it, and still has it 320 years later.

misconception.belief: Gibraltar has always been British.
misconception.correction: It was Muslim-ruled for about 750 years, Spanish for 242, and British since 1704. Almost every Spanish resident left when the town was stormed. Today's Gibraltarians descend from Genoese, Portuguese, Menorcan, Maltese, Jewish and Moroccan families who filled the empty town, which is why they speak llanito rather than English or Spanish.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Gibraltar shows what a naval base colony was for and how long its politics last: a rock taken to control the entrance to the Mediterranean is still, three centuries later, a live argument between two European democracies.
