namesOverTime.name: Menorca
namesOverTime.note: British documents spell it Minorca; the island's own language is Menorqui, a dialect of Catalan, which still carries English loanwords from the occupations.

modernSuccessors.name: Spain
modernSuccessors.note: Menorca is part of the Spanish autonomous community of the Balearic Islands.

geoCoverage.label: British, first time
geoCoverage.change: Britain wanted Port Mahon, the only deep natural harbour in the western Mediterranean a fleet could winter in.

geoCoverage.label: British, second time
geoCoverage.change: France returned the island at the Treaty of Paris that ended the Seven Years War, in exchange for British gains elsewhere.

geoCoverage.label: British, third time
geoCoverage.change: Britain retook the island from Spain during the French Revolutionary War, and gave it back four years later at Amiens.

acquisitions.how: James Stanhope landed with about 2,600 men in September 1708 and took Fort St Philip, which commands the mouth of Port Mahon, in a fortnight; Britain now had a harbour it could use in the western Mediterranean all year round.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Spain
counterparties.lost: Its best natural harbour in the western Mediterranean, along with Gibraltar four years earlier.

counterparties.name: The Menorcans
counterparties.lost: Nothing immediately: Stanhope guaranteed Catholic worship and the island's own institutions, which is why Menorcan resistance to British rule was mild by the standards of the century.
counterparties.note: The British governors kept the island's Universitats, its local councils, and left the church alone; this bought a quiet occupation.

people.name: James Stanhope
people.role: commanded the landing and the siege of Fort St Philip

acquisitions.how: Article XI of the same Utrecht treaty that gave Britain Gibraltar handed over 'the whole island of Minorca' with full sovereignty, so that within a decade Britain held both ends of the western Mediterranean.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Spain
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over Minorca in law as well as in fact; Spain spent the next ninety years trying to get it back, and eventually did.

acquisitions.how: France handed Minorca back at the Treaty of Paris that ended the Seven Years War, having held it for seven years; Britain kept Canada and Florida in the same treaty and gave France back Guadeloupe and Martinique.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of France
counterparties.lost: An island it had taken in 1756 and used as a bargaining chip; France judged the sugar of Guadeloupe worth more than the harbour of Mahon.

acquisitions.how: Charles Stuart landed at Addaia on 7 November 1798 with about 800 men, marched across the island and took it from a larger Spanish garrison in eight days without losing a man, giving Nelson a base for the blockade of Malta.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Spain
counterparties.lost: The island it had won back in 1782, after sixteen years.

people.name: Charles Stuart
people.role: commanded the 1798 landing; his bloodless capture of the island is one of the neatest operations of the war

statusPeriods.label: Naval base under a military governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Lieutenant Governor at Mahon ran the island through its existing Catholic parish and town institutions; the point of the place was the fleet anchorage, and the governors were told not to provoke the islanders.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Mahon (Mao), under the Secretary of State
statusPeriods.franchise: Menorcans elected their own town councils, the Universitats, and had no voice at all in British decisions about the island.
statusPeriods.note: Richard Kane, Lieutenant Governor for most of 1712-36, built the road across the island that is still called the Cami d'en Kane and is remembered locally with something close to affection.

statusPeriods.label: British again, after seven French years
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The same arrangement resumed: a governor at Mahon, the fleet in the harbour, and Menorcan institutions left alone. Britain spent heavily rebuilding Fort St Philip and lost it anyway.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Mahon
statusPeriods.gapReason: France held Minorca from June 1756 to February 1763 and governed it from Ciutadella, restoring the old Spanish capital.

statusPeriods.label: British for the last time
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A short third occupation, run as a fleet base for the Mediterranean campaign against Napoleon, ending when the Peace of Amiens traded it away.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Mahon
statusPeriods.gapReason: Spain held Minorca from February 1782 to November 1798, confirmed by the Treaty of Versailles in 1783.

departures.how: A French army besieged Fort St Philip for ten weeks; Admiral John Byng's fleet fought an indecisive action off the island and withdrew, the garrison surrendered on 29 June 1756, and Byng was court-martialled and shot on his own quarterdeck the following March.

led.name: John Byng
led.role: British admiral executed for 'failing to do his utmost' to relieve Minorca

led.name: William Blakeney
led.role: 84-year-old Lieutenant Governor who held Fort St Philip for ten weeks and was made a peer for it

led.name: Louis-Francois-Armand de Vignerot du Plessis, Duc de Richelieu
led.role: commanded the French expedition that took the island

cost.note: Several hundred British and Franco-Spanish soldiers died in the siege of Fort St Philip, and one British admiral was shot by his own navy. No count of Menorcan civilian deaths was made.

departures.borders: Nothing moved on land. The island changed flag whole, as it did four more times in the next forty-six years.

departures.how: A Franco-Spanish army under the Duc de Crillon blockaded Fort St Philip for six months while Britain was losing the American war; scurvy destroyed the garrison, and General James Murray surrendered with fewer than 600 men still able to stand.

led.name: James Murray
led.role: Governor who surrendered the fort when scurvy had reduced the garrison to a few hundred fit men

led.name: Louis des Balbes de Berton de Crillon
led.role: commanded the Franco-Spanish siege

cost.note: The garrison lost far more men to scurvy than to enemy fire; contemporary accounts say only a few hundred of about 2,700 were fit for duty at the surrender. Spain then demolished Fort St Philip.

departures.borders: The island passed whole to Spain and was confirmed as Spanish by the Treaty of Versailles in September 1783.

departures.how: Britain handed Minorca back to Spain at the Peace of Amiens, keeping Trinidad and Ceylon instead; the island had been British for a total of 71 of the previous 94 years and was never British again.

led.name: Henry Addington
led.role: Prime Minister whose government made the peace and gave up Minorca

led.name: Charles IV of Spain
led.role: recovered the island by treaty rather than by war

cost.note: Nobody died in the transfer. The cost had been paid in the three sieges; the handover itself was a clause in a treaty.

departures.borders: Unchanged. Menorca went back to Spain with the same coastline, and the British-built roads, sash windows and gin distilleries stayed.

consequences.economicLegacy: Port Mahon boomed on naval money and collapsed each time the fleet left; the island's gin, distilled since the eighteenth century for British sailors, is still made and still called gin.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Menorcan Catalan absorbed English words that are still in use — grevi for gravy, boinder for a bow window, xoc for chalk — and Georgian sash windows survive in the streets of Mao.
consequences.borderLegacy: None: the island returned to Spain intact, and the only line Britain drew there was a road.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 30,000 Menorcans through the eighteenth century, by British and Spanish counts that do not fully agree; the naval garrison sometimes added several thousand more.

evidence.author: Desmond Gregory
evidence.work: Minorca, the Illusory Prize: A History of the British Occupations of Minorca between 1708 and 1802
evidence.supports: All three occupations, the governors, and the island's own institutions under British rule.

evidence.author: N. A. M. Rodger
evidence.work: The Command of the Ocean: A Naval History of Britain, 1649-1815
evidence.supports: Why Port Mahon mattered strategically, and the loss of the island in 1756 and the Byng court martial.

pedagogy.hook: Minorca changed hands five times in 94 years, and Britain shot one of its own admirals for losing it.

misconception.belief: The empire grew steadily until it began to shrink after 1945.
misconception.correction: Minorca was British in 1708, French in 1756, British in 1763, Spanish in 1782, British in 1798 and Spanish for good in 1802. Territory left the empire constantly — by defeat, by treaty and by swap — for two centuries before decolonisation started.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Minorca is the clearest proof that the pink map was a poster and not a description. It also shows what the eighteenth-century empire was actually for: harbours, not land.

keyDates.what: Stanhope takes Fort St Philip
Utrecht cedes Minorca with Gibraltar
Admiral Byng shot for losing the island
Spain retakes Minorca after a six-month siege
Peace of Amiens returns it to Spain for good

territories.name: Malta
territories.formalName: The Colony of Malta and its Dependencies

namesOverTime.name: Malta
namesOverTime.note: Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and the only one that is an official language of the European Union; the islands were ruled by the Knights of St John from 1530 to 1798.

modernSuccessors.name: Malta
modernSuccessors.note: A Commonwealth realm until it became a republic on 13 December 1974; a member of the European Union since 2004.

geoCoverage.label: Malta, Gozo and Comino
geoCoverage.change: 316 square kilometres of limestone with the best harbour between Gibraltar and Alexandria, which is the reason Britain wanted it and the reason it was bombed for two years.

acquisitions.how: Maltese villagers rose against Napoleon's garrison in September 1798 and besieged it in Valletta for two years with British, Portuguese and Neapolitan help; when the starving French surrendered on 5 September 1800 they surrendered to the British, who then stayed.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: An island Napoleon had seized from the Knights of St John in June 1798 on his way to Egypt, and a garrison of about 3,000 men.

counterparties.name: The Maltese national congress
counterparties.lost: The self-government they had fought for. The Maltese leaders who organised the blockade expected a share in ruling the islands; they got a British civil commissioner and no assembly for 121 years.
counterparties.note: In 1802 a Maltese deputation issued a Declaration of Rights asserting that the islanders had freely chosen the British Crown and that no power could give them away without their consent. Britain accepted the sovereignty and ignored the condition.

people.name: Emmanuele Vitale
people.role: notary of Rabat who commanded the Maltese insurgents against the French

people.name: Canon Francesco Saverio Caruana
people.role: priest and leader of the Maltese national congress, later Bishop of Malta

people.name: Alexander Ball
people.role: Royal Navy captain who led the blockade and became the first British civil commissioner; the Maltese put up a monument to him

acquisitions.resistance: The resistance was against the French, not the British: a two-year siege in which Maltese irregulars did most of the fighting and suffered most of the hunger.

acquisitions.how: The Treaty of Amiens in 1802 had promised Malta back to the Knights of St John; Britain never left, and the Treaty of Paris in 1814 recognised the islands as British 'in full right and sovereignty' with the agreement of the powers and no vote by the Maltese.

counterparties.name: The Order of St John
counterparties.lost: The islands it had ruled since 1530 and lost to Napoleon in 1798; the Order survives as a sovereign entity in Rome with no territory.

counterparties.name: The Maltese
counterparties.lost: Any say in the transfer. The 1802 declaration that they had chosen Britain freely was not mentioned in the treaty.

statusPeriods.label: Occupied, with the future undecided
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British civil commissioner governed alongside the Maltese congress while London decided whether to keep the islands, hand them back to the Knights, or trade them; the Maltese were told at different times that all three were about to happen.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Valletta, under the Secretary of State for War and the Colonies

statusPeriods.label: Fortress colony of the Mediterranean Fleet
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Sir Thomas Maitland arrived as the first Governor with almost unlimited powers, abolished the Maltese congress and ruled by proclamation; the dockyard and the fleet were the economy, and the Governor was answerable only to London.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Palace, Valletta
statusPeriods.franchise: A council with a small elected element was allowed from 1849 and could always be outvoted by official members. The language question — Italian, English or Maltese in the courts and schools — dominated politics for a century.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government, granted after four men were shot
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After British troops killed four demonstrators in Valletta on 7 June 1919, Britain gave Malta a parliament with control of internal affairs while keeping defence, foreign policy and the dockyard.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Valletta, with a Maltese Prime Minister and a British Governor
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male suffrage; women could not vote until 1947.
statusPeriods.note: The constitution was suspended in 1930 during a quarrel between the government and the Catholic Church, restored in 1932, and revoked outright in 1933 when the Maltese government spent money on Italian teaching against London's wishes.

statusPeriods.label: Direct rule again, then the siege
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Governor ruled directly for fourteen years, which included the two years when Malta was the most heavily bombed place on earth; Maltese politicians who favoured Italy were interned and deported to Uganda in 1942.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Valletta

statusPeriods.label: Self-government, integration, then independence
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A 1947 constitution restored a Maltese parliament with universal suffrage, including women for the first time; it was suspended again from 1958 to 1962 after the integration talks collapsed and Dom Mintoff resigned.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Valletta
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from 1947, women included.

departures.how: After integration with Britain was offered, voted for and then dropped, Malta negotiated independence at a London conference, approved the constitution in a referendum in May 1964, and became a state on 21 September with British forces still in the harbour under a ten-year defence agreement.

led.name: Giorgio Borg Olivier
led.role: Prime Minister who negotiated and took independence

led.name: Dom Mintoff
led.role: Labour leader who had campaigned for full integration with Britain, then for a republic; boycotted the independence constitution and later expelled British forces

led.name: Duncan Sandys
led.role: Secretary of State for the Colonies who chaired the independence conference

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The costs had come earlier: four demonstrators shot in 1919, about 1,500 civilians killed in the wartime siege, and mass emigration in the 1950s when the dockyard was run down.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. An archipelago of three inhabited islands became a state with the coastline it had always had, and Britain kept base rights, not territory.

instrument.name: Malta Independence Act 1964
instrument.note: Royal assent 31 July 1964; independence took effect on 21 September 1964.

evidence.author: Henry Frendo
evidence.work: Party Politics in a Fortress Colony: The Maltese Experience
evidence.supports: The integration debate, the parties, and the road to independence.

violence.note: British troops shot dead four Maltese demonstrators during bread riots in Valletta on 7 June 1919, a date Malta now keeps as a national holiday; the 1940-42 siege killed about 1,500 civilians.

populationTransfer.note: The run-down of the dockyard drove one of the highest emigration rates in Europe: about 140,000 Maltese left between 1946 and 1979, mostly for Australia, Canada and Britain, from a population of around 300,000.

commonwealth.note: Malta became a republic on 13 December 1974 and stayed in the Commonwealth. The last British forces left on 31 March 1979, which Malta marks as Freedom Day.

consequences.economicLegacy: The naval dockyard was the economy for 150 years, employing about 12,000 Maltese at its peak; when Britain wound it down the island had to invent tourism, manufacturing and finance instead.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English is still an official language alongside Maltese; the courts use a code partly Napoleonic and partly English, and driving is on the left.

peak.populationNote: The 1967 census, three years after independence. Malta is one of the most densely populated countries in the world and was so under British rule too.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Malta’s largest recorded population: 314,216 people, counted in 1967.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Malta’s greatest extent, 316 km² in 1964: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 326 km², within 3.2% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Henry Frendo
evidence.work: Party Politics in a Fortress Colony: The Maltese Experience
evidence.supports: Maltese politics under British rule, the language question, and the integration and independence campaigns.

evidence.author: Brian Blouet
evidence.work: The Story of Malta
evidence.supports: The general narrative from the Knights through the British period.

evidence.author: Ernle Bradford
evidence.work: Siege: Malta 1940-1943
evidence.supports: The wartime siege, the convoys and the civilian cost.

contested.note: Whether the 1956 integration referendum showed a real Maltese desire to join Britain is argued: 74% of those voting said yes, but the Nationalist Party and the Church urged abstention and turnout was under 60%, so integrationists and Nationalists can each quote a number that suits them.

pedagogy.hook: In 1956 Malta voted to become part of the United Kingdom, with its own MPs at Westminster. Britain lost interest, and eight years later Malta chose independence instead.

misconception.belief: Every colony wanted independence from Britain as soon as it could get it.
misconception.correction: Malta's Labour leader Dom Mintoff campaigned for integration: Maltese MPs in the Commons, British wage rates and British welfare. The February 1956 referendum passed with about 74% of votes cast, though turnout was under 60% because the Nationalists and the Church called for abstention. Britain would not pay for parity, and the plan died.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Malta shows that the alternatives to empire were not only independence: some colonised people asked to be let all the way in, and were refused because it would have cost money.

keyDates.what: The French garrison surrenders to Britain
Treaty of Paris makes Malta British
Sette Giugno: troops shoot four demonstrators
The George Cross awarded to the whole island
Referendum votes to join the United Kingdom
Independence under Borg Olivier

territories.name: The Ionian Islands
territories.formalName: The United States of the Ionian Islands, under British protection

namesOverTime.name: United States of the Ionian Islands
namesOverTime.note: Seven islands — Corfu, Paxos, Lefkada, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Kythira — called by the Greeks the Eptanisa, the Seven Islands.

geoCoverage.label: The Seven Islands
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the smaller islands in 1809-10 but Corfu, the largest and the one with the fortress, held out under its French garrison until 1814, so the drawn shape is only partly British for five years.

acquisitions.how: A British expedition under John Oswald took Zakynthos, Cephalonia, Ithaca and Kythira from their French garrisons in a few days in October 1809, adding Lefkada in 1810; Corfu's French garrison held out until Napoleon fell and surrendered in June 1814.

counterparties.name: The French Empire
counterparties.lost: Seven islands that had been Venetian for four centuries, briefly a Russo-Ottoman republic, and French since 1807.

counterparties.name: The Ionian islanders
counterparties.lost: The Septinsular Republic of 1800-07, the first Greek self-governing state of modern times, which had been abolished by France and was not restored by Britain.
counterparties.note: Many islanders welcomed the British as a change from French conscription and taxation. What they wanted was self-rule, and later union with Greece.

people.name: John Oswald
people.role: commanded the 1809 expedition that took the southern islands

acquisitions.how: The powers meeting after Waterloo made the seven islands a single state under the 'immediate and exclusive protection' of Britain: a republic on paper with a British Lord High Commissioner who appointed its senate, controlled its police and censored its press.

counterparties.name: The Ionian islanders
counterparties.lost: The independence the treaty appeared to give them. The 1817 constitution written by Thomas Maitland put every real power in the Lord High Commissioner's hands and lasted until 1849.

counterparties.name: The Austrian Empire and the other powers
counterparties.lost: A claim on the islands; Austria in particular wanted them and settled for a British protectorate rather than let anyone else have them.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris (5 November 1815) on the Ionian Islands

people.name: Sir Thomas Maitland
people.role: first Lord High Commissioner, known to the islanders as 'King Tom'; wrote the 1817 constitution that gave himself the power

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation during the war
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British commanders governed the captured islands under martial authority while the war went on and Corfu remained French; there was no settled legal status until the powers made one in 1815.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Zakynthos, then Corfu

statusPeriods.label: A 'free state' with a British Lord High Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Lord High Commissioner nominated the senate, licensed the newspapers, commanded the police and could dissolve the assembly, which he did whenever it voted for union with Greece; the islands paid for a garrison they did not command.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Palace of St Michael and St George, Corfu
statusPeriods.franchise: A narrow property franchise under the 1817 constitution, widened by the 1849 reforms; once elections were freer, the assembly voted for union with Greece and kept voting for it.
statusPeriods.note: Britain built roads, a water supply for Corfu, courts and the Ionian Academy, the first Greek-language university. It also flogged and hanged rebels in Cephalonia in 1849 under martial law.

departures.how: Britain gave the seven islands to Greece as a welcome present for its new king, blew up the fortifications of Corfu on the way out, and became the only European power of the century to hand a colony to a neighbouring state because its people had voted, repeatedly, to go.

led.name: Ioannis Typaldos-Kapodistrias
led.role: leader of the Rizospastai, the Radical Unionists who campaigned in the Ionian assembly for union with Greece

led.name: Iosif Momferratos
led.role: Radical Unionist deputy, exiled by the British administration for his campaigning

led.name: William Ewart Gladstone
led.role: sent as Lord High Commissioner Extraordinary in 1858 to find a reform that would keep the islands British, and concluded there was none

led.name: Henry Storks
led.role: last Lord High Commissioner, who handed the islands over

departures.movement: The Rizospastai (Radical Unionists) and the campaign for enosis with Greece

cost.note: Nobody died in the handover. The deaths belong to the Cephalonia peasant rising of 1849, when Lord High Commissioner Henry Ward's courts martial hanged 21 men and flogged hundreds; some accounts put the executions higher, and the number of deaths in the fighting itself is not known.

departures.borders: The islands went to Greece whole and no line was drawn. Britain's only condition was that Corfu and Paxos be neutralised and their Venetian fortresses demolished, which British engineers did before leaving.

instrument.name: Treaty of London (1864)
instrument.note: Signed by Britain, France and Russia in March 1864; the British flag came down in Corfu and the troops sailed on 2 June 1864.

contested.note: Whether Britain left because the islanders demanded it or because the islands had stopped being strategically useful once Malta and the overland route to India mattered more is argued. Both explanations are in the Foreign Office papers of the time.

consequences.economicLegacy: The currant trade of Zakynthos and Cephalonia boomed under British rule and collapsed when French vineyards recovered; roads, lighthouses and Corfu's water supply were the lasting British investments.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Corfu still plays cricket on the Spianada, drinks tsitsibira, a local ginger beer, and uses Italian and English loanwords; the Ionian Academy, founded in 1824, was the first university in the Greek world.

peak.populationNote: About 230,000 people on the seven islands at the cession in 1864, by the protectorate's own returns, which were reasonably careful because they were used for taxation.

evidence.author: Thomas W. Gallant
evidence.work: Experiencing Dominion: Culture, Identity, and Power in the British Mediterranean
evidence.supports: How British rule worked on the ground in the Ionian Islands, and the Cephalonia risings.

evidence.author: Robert Holland and Diana Markides
evidence.work: The British and the Hellenes: Struggles for Mastery in the Eastern Mediterranean 1850-1960
evidence.supports: The cession of 1864 and its place in a longer British argument with Greek national feeling that ran on to Cyprus.

pedagogy.hook: Britain ruled Corfu for fifty years and gave it away in 1864 as a welcome present for the new King of Greece.

misconception.belief: Britain never gave up territory unless it was defeated or forced out.
misconception.correction: The Ionian Islands were handed to Greece in 1864 because their assembly kept voting for union and holding them had become embarrassing. Gladstone was sent in 1858 to find a reform that would keep them British and reported that there was none. Britain demolished Corfu's fortresses and left.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Ionian protectorate is the model that failed: a colony dressed as a free state, with a constitution, a flag and a parliament that could not do anything. When the parliament became genuinely elected, it voted itself out of the empire.

keyDates.what: British forces take the southern islands
The protectorate is created in Paris
Cephalonia rising crushed; 21 hanged

date.note: Gladstone reached Corfu in late November 1858; sources differ on the exact day.

keyDates.what: Gladstone sent to reform the protectorate
The islands are handed to Greece

territories.name: Cyprus
territories.formalName: The Colony of Cyprus, and the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia

namesOverTime.name: Kypros / Kibris
namesOverTime.note: Ottoman from 1571. The Ottoman conquest brought the Turkish-speaking Muslim community whose descendants are the Turkish Cypriots, and restored the Orthodox Church, whose archbishop became the leader of the Greek Cypriots.

modernSuccessors.name: Republic of Cyprus
modernSuccessors.note: Divided since 1974: the Republic controls the south, and the north is administered by a Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: The third largest island in the Mediterranean, 260 kilometres from Suez and 100 from the Turkish coast, which is the whole reason Britain wanted it.

geoCoverage.label: The Sovereign Base Areas only
geoCoverage.change: Cyprus became independent and Britain kept 254 square kilometres of it — about 3% of the island — as sovereign British territory, which it still holds.

acquisitions.how: Britain promised to defend the Ottoman Empire against Russia and took Cyprus to occupy and administer in return; the Sultan kept legal sovereignty, and the island was made to pay Britain £92,800 a year, which Britain paid straight to the holders of defaulted Ottoman bonds.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Effective possession of an island whose legal title it kept for another 36 years, and the revenues of one of its provinces.

counterparties.name: The people of Cyprus
counterparties.lost: Their taxes. Cypriots were not consulted about the transfer, and for 47 years their surplus revenue serviced a Turkish debt owed largely to British and French investors; the tribute was only cancelled in 1927.
counterparties.note: Greek Cypriots greeted the British in 1878 expecting that Britain, having given the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864, would soon do the same with Cyprus. The Bishop of Kition said as much to the first British commander on the day he landed.

instrument.name: Cyprus Convention
instrument.note: A secret defensive alliance signed on 4 June 1878; British troops landed at Larnaca on 12 July.

people.name: Sir Garnet Wolseley
people.role: first High Commissioner; landed at Larnaca in July 1878

people.name: Kyprianos, Bishop of Kition
people.role: welcomed the British and asked them at once to hand the island to Greece as they had the Ionian Islands

people.name: Benjamin Disraeli
people.role: Prime Minister who took Cyprus as a 'place of arms' guarding the route to India

acquisitions.how: When the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on Germany's side, Britain annexed Cyprus outright by Order in Council; in October 1915 it offered the island to Greece if Greece would join the war, and the Greek government refused.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: The legal sovereignty it had kept since 1878. Turkey recognised the annexation in the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923.

statusPeriods.label: Occupied and administered, but legally Ottoman
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British High Commissioner governed with a Legislative Council in which the official members plus the Turkish Cypriot elected members could always outvote the Greek Cypriot majority — a design, not an accident.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nicosia, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male taxpayers voted in communal electorates: nine Greek Cypriot seats, three Turkish Cypriot, six official. The arithmetic meant the Greek Cypriot majority could never carry a vote against the government.
statusPeriods.note: The £92,800 annual 'tribute' was the central grievance of Cypriot politics for two generations: the island paid it, but not one piastre reached the Ottoman treasury.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, then counter-insurgency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Annexed in 1914 and formally made a Crown Colony on 1 May 1925, Cyprus was governed by a Governor and a council; after Greek Cypriots burned Government House in October 1931 the council was abolished and Cyprus was ruled without any elected body for a quarter of a century.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Government House, Nicosia
statusPeriods.franchise: None at colony level after 1931. Municipal elections continued; the church and the communal institutions became the only outlets for Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot politics, which shaped everything that followed.
statusPeriods.note: From 1955 to 1959 the island was under a state of emergency: about 3,000 people were detained without trial, nine EOKA members were hanged, and collective punishments were imposed on villages.

statusPeriods.label: The Sovereign Base Areas stay British
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Akrotiri and Dhekelia are administered by a British Administrator who is also the Commander of British Forces Cyprus; the roughly 7,000 Cypriots living inside them keep their Republic of Cyprus citizenship and a law that copies the Republic's.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Episkopi, under the Ministry of Defence rather than the Foreign Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Residents of the base areas vote in Republic of Cyprus elections, not British ones. There is no local legislature.
statusPeriods.note: The bases are the reason Britain is still, in law, a territorial power in the eastern Mediterranean; RAF Akrotiri has been used for operations over Iraq, Syria and Libya.

departures.how: Four years of EOKA bombings and ambushes, and a British counter-insurgency of detention without trial, curfews and nine hangings, ended in a deal made in Zurich and London between Greece, Turkey and Britain — not with EOKA — that made Cyprus independent, banned union with Greece, and kept 254 square kilometres British.

led.name: Archbishop Makarios III
led.role: leader of the Greek Cypriot enosis campaign, deported to the Seychelles in March 1956, and first President of the republic he had not asked for

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cyprus is where the British Mediterranean ends and where the pattern of a rushed, ethnically-designed constitution followed by partition — the same pattern as Ireland and India — happened for the third time.

namesOverTime.name: Helgoland
namesOverTime.note: The islanders spoke Halunder, a North Frisian dialect, and were fishermen and North Sea pilots; Denmark had held the island since 1714.

modernSuccessors.name: Germany
modernSuccessors.note: Part of Schleswig-Holstein. The island was evacuated and used as a bombing range from 1945 to 1952, and the islanders were allowed home only in March 1952.

geoCoverage.label: One red sandstone rock in the German Bight
geoCoverage.change: Less than two square kilometres of cliff and dune, 50 kilometres off the mouths of the Elbe and the Weser — worthless as land, priceless as a position.

acquisitions.how: A small Royal Navy squadron took Heligoland from its Danish garrison without a fight in September 1807, weeks after the British bombardment of Copenhagen, and turned the island into the depot through which British goods were smuggled into Napoleon's blockaded Europe.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Denmark-Norway
counterparties.lost: An island it had held since 1714, taken as part of the same campaign in which the Royal Navy bombarded Copenhagen and seized the Danish fleet.

counterparties.name: The Heligolanders
counterparties.lost: Little at first, and they gained a great deal: the smuggling trade made the island rich, and British rule left their Frisian language, their fishing rights and their tax exemptions alone.
counterparties.note: Heligoland paid no British taxes and kept its own laws and currency; the islanders' main complaint against Britain was that the Colonial Office ignored them.

acquisitions.how: Denmark, on the losing side of the Napoleonic wars, formally ceded Heligoland to Britain at the Treaty of Kiel; it was one of only three territories Britain kept in Europe from that war, with Malta and the Ionian Islands.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Denmark
counterparties.lost: Heligoland outright, and Norway to Sweden in the same treaty.

statusPeriods.label: A smugglers' depot under naval occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Royal Navy held the island and licensed the merchants who ran British cloth, coffee, sugar and colonial goods across to the German coast in defiance of Napoleon's Continental System.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The naval command, under the Admiralty

statusPeriods.label: A two-square-kilometre crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Lieutenant Governor and a handful of officials ran an island of about 2,000 fishermen and pilots; there were no British taxes, no conscription, and after 1826 a fashionable sea-bathing resort and a casino.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Government House, Heligoland, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: The islanders elected their own local council, which quarrelled with the Lieutenant Governor for most of the century over who controlled the gambling licences.
statusPeriods.note: Heligoland was a refuge for German liberals after the failed revolutions of 1848, and August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben wrote the words of the German national anthem there in August 1841, on British soil.

departures.how: Britain gave Heligoland to Germany in exchange for German recognition of a British protectorate over Zanzibar and a free hand in what became Kenya and Uganda; the roughly 2,000 islanders were not consulted, and the German navy began fortifying the rock at once.

led.name: Lord Salisbury
led.role: Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary who made the exchange and thought a North Sea rock cheap for a quarter of East Africa

led.name: Leo von Caprivi
led.role: German Chancellor who negotiated the agreement in Bismarck's place

led.name: Kaiser Wilhelm II
led.role: wanted the island for the navy and got it

cost.note: Nobody died in the transfer. The bill came later: in 1945 the RAF dropped nearly 7,000 tonnes of bombs on the island, and on 18 April 1947 the Royal Navy detonated about 6,700 tonnes of surplus explosive there in one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever set off.

departures.borders: An island changed states whole, and the borders that moved were in Africa: the same agreement drew the boundary between British and German East Africa and left the straight line that still separates Kenya from Tanzania.

instrument.name: Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty (Anglo-German Agreement of 1890)
instrument.note: Signed on 1 July 1890; the handover ceremony on Heligoland took place on 9 August.

contested.note: German nationalists denounced the treaty as giving away Africa for a bathtub; British critics said Salisbury had handed Germany the key to the North Sea. Historians still disagree about whether the exchange strengthened or weakened Britain's position in 1914.

evidence.author: Jan Ruger
evidence.work: Heligoland: Britain, Germany, and the Struggle for the North Sea
evidence.supports: The whole arc from the 1807 seizure to the 1890 exchange and the island's later fate.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1890 agreement that gave away Heligoland also drew the Anglo-German boundary in East Africa, and the line it fixed is now the border between Kenya and Tanzania.
consequences.economicLegacy: Napoleonic smuggling made the island briefly rich, sea-bathing kept it prosperous, and German naval fortification ended civilian life on it for good.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Halunder, the islanders' North Frisian dialect, survived British rule intact and is still spoken by a few hundred people; British rule left almost no legal trace.

peak.populationNote: About 2,000 Heligolanders in 1890, most of them fishermen, boatmen and pilots for the Elbe and Weser trade, plus several thousand summer visitors to the bathing resort.

evidence.author: Jan Ruger
evidence.work: Heligoland: Britain, Germany, and the Struggle for the North Sea
evidence.supports: British rule on the island, the 1890 exchange, and what Germany then did with it.

evidence.author: Ronald Hyam
evidence.work: Britain's Imperial Century, 1815-1914: A Study of Empire and Expansion
evidence.supports: Where the Heligoland-Zanzibar exchange fits in the scramble for Africa and Salisbury's strategy.

pedagogy.hook: The words of the German national anthem were written on a British island, and 49 years later Britain traded that island to Germany for Zanzibar.

misconception.belief: Britain only ever took territory; it never gave any away.
misconception.correction: In 1890 Britain handed Heligoland to Germany to buy German recognition of British claims over Zanzibar, Kenya and Uganda. Lord Salisbury thought a two-square-kilometre North Sea rock a cheap price for a quarter of East Africa. German engineers then turned the rock into the fortress that guarded the High Seas Fleet.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Heligoland shows how the scramble for Africa was actually conducted: not at the Berlin conference, but in bilateral bargains where a European island could be exchanged for a slice of a continent whose people were consulted about none of it.

namesOverTime.name: Regnu di Corsica
namesOverTime.note: The kingdom's own language of government was Italian, not English or French.

modernSuccessors.name: France
modernSuccessors.note: Corsica is a territorial collectivity of France with a limited devolved assembly.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: For twenty-eight months the fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean was a kingdom whose king lived in Windsor and had never seen it.

acquisitions.how: Pasquale Paoli, in revolt against the French Republic, invited the Royal Navy in; British and Corsican troops took San Fiorenzo, Bastia and Calvi, where Nelson lost the sight of his right eye, and a Corsican assembly at Corte then offered the crown to George III.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: An island France had bought from Genoa in 1768 and conquered a year later, and the base from which its fleet worked the western Mediterranean.

counterparties.name: Pasquale Paoli and the Corsican independence movement
counterparties.lost: The self-rule they had asked Britain to protect. Paoli wanted a British protector; he got a British viceroy, Sir Gilbert Elliot, who governed over his head, and in October 1795 Paoli was eased onto a ship to London on a British pension and died there in 1807.
counterparties.note: Paoli had already led an independent Corsican republic from 1755 to 1769, with a written constitution that Rousseau admired, before France crushed it.

instrument.name: The Anglo-Corsican constitution adopted by the consulta at Corte
instrument.note: The assembly offered the crown to George III on terms: a Corsican parliament, Corsican as the language of the island's business, and the Catholic religion guaranteed.

people.name: Pasquale Paoli
people.role: Corsican national leader who invited the British in and was then removed by them

people.name: Sir Gilbert Elliot
people.role: Viceroy of Corsica, who governed the kingdom and evacuated it

people.name: Horatio Nelson
people.role: commanded batteries at Bastia and Calvi and lost the sight of his right eye at Calvi in July 1794

people.name: Carlo Andrea Pozzo di Borgo
people.role: Corsican who became president of the kingdom's council of state, and later a Russian diplomat and lifelong enemy of Bonaparte

acquisitions.resistance: The French garrisons held Bastia and Calvi through long sieges; there was no general Corsican resistance to the British because most Corsicans in arms were on their side.

statusPeriods.label: The Anglo-Corsican Kingdom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: George III was King of Corsica; a Viceroy appointed in London governed with a single-chamber Corsican parliament that voted taxes and argued with him about almost everything else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bastia, under a Viceroy appointed by the Crown
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1794 constitution gave the vote to Corsican men meeting a small property qualification — wide for its time, and irrelevant within two years.
statusPeriods.note: The kingdom's business was conducted in Italian. It is the only time a British monarch has been the constitutional king of a Mediterranean state with its own parliament.

departures.how: Spain's entry into the war and Bonaparte's victories in Italy made the island indefensible; Gilbert Elliot evacuated the garrison from Bastia in October 1796 without a battle, and French troops landed as the British sailed, so the kingdom ended by abandonment rather than by treaty.

led.name: Sir Gilbert Elliot
led.role: Viceroy who ordered and organised the evacuation

led.name: Horatio Nelson
led.role: covered the evacuation of Bastia with his squadron

led.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
led.role: Corsican-born commander of the French army in Italy whose victories made the island untenable for Britain

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the evacuation itself. Several hundred died in the sieges of Bastia and Calvi in 1794, and Corsicans who had supported the kingdom faced French reprisals afterwards.

departures.borders: None. The island returned to France whole and has been French ever since; not one line on any map was moved by the twenty-eight-month kingdom.

contested.note: There is no departure category in this model for 'walked away'. Britain did not cede Corsica or lose it in battle: it evacuated, and France reoccupied. The record uses transfer-to-another-power because it is the nearest term, and says here that it is not exact.

consequences.economicLegacy: Two years were not enough to change anything. The kingdom left no institutions, no roads and no trade.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Corsican and Italian remained the languages of the island; French replaced them in the nineteenth century, long after the British had gone.

peak.populationNote: About 150,000 Corsicans in the 1790s, by French counts made shortly before and after the British period.

pedagogy.hook: For twenty-eight months George III was King of Corsica — and Napoleon Bonaparte, born on the island, was fighting on the other side.

misconception.belief: The British Empire was in Africa, Asia and the Americas, not in Europe.
misconception.correction: Britain ruled Corsica in 1794-96, Minorca three times, Malta, the Ionian Islands, Heligoland and Cyprus, and occupied Iceland and the Faroe Islands in 1940. The European possessions were harbours with people attached, held to keep the route to India open.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Corsica is the shortest colony in this atlas and shows the pattern in miniature: a local leader invites an outside power in against a bigger enemy, and finds that the protector governs.

territories.name: Iceland
territories.formalName: The Kingdom of Iceland, under British military occupation

modernSuccessors.name: Iceland
modernSuccessors.note: Iceland was a sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark from 1918 and declared itself a republic on 17 June 1944, while still under American occupation.

geoCoverage.label: Occupied, but self-governed
geoCoverage.change: British troops held the ports, the airfields and the wireless stations. The Icelandic government went on running the country, which is why the unit is drawn as partial control rather than as territory.

acquisitions.how: 746 Royal Marines landed at Reykjavik at dawn on 10 May 1940, a month after Germany occupied Denmark, and took over a neutral country that had no army, no navy and four unarmed policemen on the quay to meet them.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Iceland
counterparties.lost: Its neutrality. Iceland was a sovereign state that had declared permanent neutrality in 1918; Britain invaded it because Germany might, and the Icelandic government formally protested the violation before agreeing to cooperate.
counterparties.note: Iceland had refused a British request to join the Allies in April 1940. The invasion followed the refusal by three weeks.

people.name: Hermann Jonasson
people.role: Prime Minister of Iceland, who protested the invasion, told Icelanders to treat the troops as guests, and negotiated the American takeover

people.name: Robert Sturges
people.role: colonel of Royal Marines who commanded the landing force

people.name: Sveinn Bjornsson
people.role: regent of Iceland during the occupation and first President of the republic in 1944

acquisitions.resistance: None. Iceland had no armed forces. The Reykjavik police directed traffic for the landing parties, and the British commander had leaflets printed apologising for the inconvenience.

statusPeriods.label: British military occupation of a neutral democracy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Althing and the Icelandic government continued to legislate and govern; the British commander controlled the harbours, censorship and movement, and had no civil authority at all.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default degree of 5 for 'occupied' assumes military government. Here there was none: Iceland's own parliament and ministers ran the country throughout, and Britain controlled only defence, shipping and censorship.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Reykjavik, by the Icelandic government, with a British force commander alongside
statusPeriods.franchise: Icelanders kept their own universal suffrage and held elections during the occupation.
statusPeriods.note: At its height the garrison numbered around 25,000 British and Canadian troops on an island of about 121,000 people.

departures.how: Britain needed the troops elsewhere and Roosevelt wanted a foothold in the Atlantic: on 7 July 1941, five months before Pearl Harbor, United States marines relieved the British garrison by agreement with the Icelandic government, and Britain's occupation of a European democracy ended by subcontracting it.

becomes.name: Iceland, occupied by the United States

led.name: Hermann Jonasson
led.role: Prime Minister who negotiated the terms of the American arrival, including a promise to withdraw at the end of the war

led.name: Winston Churchill
led.role: wanted the British garrison released for other theatres and pressed Washington to take it over

led.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
led.role: sent US marines to a neutral country while the United States was still formally neutral

cost.note: No Icelander was killed by the occupying force in 1940 and none in the handover. Iceland's war dead were merchant seamen and fishermen carrying fish to Britain through the U-boat campaign; the boom in wages and fish prices is remembered in Iceland as 'the blessed war'.

departures.borders: None. Iceland's territory was untouched, and the occupation hastened the end of its union with Denmark: the country declared itself a republic on 17 June 1944, while American troops were still there.

instrument.name: The Icelandic-American defence agreement of July 1941
instrument.note: Iceland agreed to the American arrival in return for a promise of withdrawal at the end of the war and recognition of its full independence. The United States kept a base at Keflavik until 2006.

consequences.economicLegacy: The occupation ended Iceland's depression: British and then American spending, and wartime fish prices, built harbours, roads and the airfield at Keflavik, which became the country's international airport.
consequences.borderLegacy: None on land. The postwar dispute was at sea: Iceland and Britain fought three 'Cod Wars' between 1958 and 1976 over fishing limits, and Iceland won every one of them.

peak.populationNote: About 121,000 Icelanders in 1940. The Allied garrison at its peak was roughly a quarter to a third of that number, which is why the occupation reshaped the economy so completely.

evidence.author: Donald F. Bittner
evidence.work: The Lion and the White Falcon: Britain and Iceland in the World War II Era
evidence.supports: The invasion, the occupation administration, and the handover to the United States.

evidence.author: Gunnar Karlsson
evidence.work: The History of Iceland
evidence.supports: Iceland's constitutional position in 1940 and the wartime road to the republic of 1944.

pedagogy.hook: In May 1940 Britain invaded a neutral democracy that had no army, and handed out leaflets apologising for the inconvenience.

misconception.belief: In the Second World War Britain only ever defended other countries' neutrality; it never violated it.
misconception.correction: Britain invaded neutral Iceland on 10 May 1940 and the neutral Faroe Islands on 12 April 1940, because Germany had taken Denmark and the North Atlantic convoy route mattered more than neutrality. The Icelandic government protested formally, then cooperated, and Britain handed the occupation to the United States in 1941.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Iceland is the clearest case of occupation without colonisation: Britain took the island's strategic position and left its government alone, which is exactly what a naval empire wanted and rarely got so cheaply.

territories.name: The Faroe Islands
territories.formalName: The Faroe Islands, under British military occupation

modernSuccessors.name: Denmark (Faroe Islands)
modernSuccessors.note: Self-governing within the Kingdom of Denmark under the Home Rule Act of 1948; the Faroes are outside the European Union even though Denmark is in it.

geoCoverage.label: Occupied, and left to govern themselves
geoCoverage.change: Eighteen islands in the North Atlantic, occupied for their position on the convoy routes and for the airfield the British built at Vagar.

acquisitions.how: Three days after Germany occupied Denmark, HMS Suffolk landed Royal Marines at Torshavn; Britain took the islands to keep them out of German hands, and told the Faroese it was a temporary protection and not an annexation.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Denmark
counterparties.lost: Control of a dependency it could no longer reach or supply, since Denmark itself was under German occupation.

counterparties.name: The Faroese
counterparties.lost: Their neutrality, and about one in every 250 of their people at sea. What they gained was a flag: Britain recognised the Merkid in April 1940 so that Faroese boats would not be sunk as Danish ones.
counterparties.note: The recognition of the flag mattered far beyond the war: 25 April is still celebrated in the Faroes as Flag Day.

people.name: Carl Aage Hilbert
people.role: Danish prefect who stayed and governed the islands through the occupation, cut off from his own government

people.name: Thorstein Petersen
people.role: Faroese People's Party leader who pressed for separation from Denmark during and after the occupation

acquisitions.resistance: None. The Logting protested the landing formally and then worked with the British, who left civil government entirely in Faroese and Danish hands.

statusPeriods.label: The friendly occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Danish prefect and the Faroese Logting continued to govern and even to legislate for themselves for the first time; the British controlled shipping, censorship and defence, and built an airfield at Vagar.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default degree of 5 for 'occupied' assumes military government. Britain imposed none: the islands' own institutions gained powers during the occupation rather than losing them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Torshavn, by the prefect and the Logting, with a British force commander alongside
statusPeriods.franchise: Faroese adult suffrage continued; the Logting legislated on its own authority for the first time because Copenhagen could not be reached.

departures.how: British forces left in September 1945 and the islands returned to Denmark; the Faroese, who had governed themselves and flown their own flag for five years, voted narrowly for independence in September 1946, and Denmark dissolved the Logting and offered home rule instead.

led.name: Thorstein Petersen
led.role: led the campaign for separation and won the 1946 referendum by a narrow margin that Denmark did not accept

led.name: Carl Aage Hilbert
led.role: Danish prefect who handed the islands back to Copenhagen's authority

led.name: Clement Attlee
led.role: Prime Minister whose government withdrew the garrison and declined to take a view on the islands' future

cost.note: Faroese sources give figures between about 130 and 210 seamen and fishermen killed carrying fish to Britain, from roughly 25 ships lost. Proportionally it was one of the heaviest civilian losses of any Allied population, and the counts differ over whether fishing and merchant crews are combined.

departures.borders: None moved. The Faroes went back to Denmark with the same eighteen islands, and the flag Britain recognised in 1940 is the flag they fly today.

contested.note: The September 1946 referendum produced a narrow majority for separation on a low turnout. Denmark dissolved the Logting rather than accept the result, and the home rule settlement of 1948 followed. Faroese and Danish accounts of whether the vote was valid still differ.

consequences.economicLegacy: Wartime fish prices in Britain made the islands prosperous and paid for the modern fishing fleet; the airfield the RAF built at Vagar is still the Faroes' only airport.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Faroese was used in government during the occupation because Copenhagen was unreachable, and never fully gave the ground back; the flag Britain recognised in 1940 became the emblem of home rule.

peak.populationNote: About 29,000 Faroese during the occupation, with a British garrison of a few thousand.

evidence.author: Jonathan Wylie
evidence.work: The Faroe Islands: Interpretations of History
evidence.supports: The islands' constitutional relationship with Denmark and the effect of the occupation on Faroese self-government.

contested.note: The number of Faroese seamen killed in the war and the standing of the 1946 independence referendum are both given differently in Faroese and Danish accounts. The British occupation itself is well documented and not disputed.

pedagogy.hook: Britain invaded the Faroe Islands in 1940 and gave them their flag: London recognised the Merkid so Faroese boats would not be sunk as Danish ones.

misconception.belief: Occupation always means oppression.
misconception.correction: The Faroese call it the friendly occupation. Fish prices soared, Faroese became the language of government because Copenhagen was unreachable, and the separate flag Britain recognised became the emblem of a home-rule movement that won in 1948. It was still an invasion of a neutral people who were never asked.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Faroes show that occupations can strengthen the occupied: five years of enforced self-government produced a national movement that Denmark then had to bargain with.

keyDates.what: Royal Marines land at Torshavn
Britain recognises the Faroese flag; now Flag Day
British forces leave
Narrow referendum vote for independence, not accepted
Home rule within Denmark instead

territories.name: Madeira
territories.formalName: The Portuguese island of Madeira, twice under British occupation

geoCoverage.label: First occupation
geoCoverage.change: A British garrison landed at Funchal to keep the island out of French and Spanish hands while Portugal was under pressure to close its ports to Britain.

to.note: The garrison was withdrawn during 1814 after the war ended; contemporary accounts give the month differently.

geoCoverage.label: Second occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain landed troops on the day Napoleon's army reached Lisbon, and held the island for seven years while the Portuguese court governed its empire from Brazil.

acquisitions.how: British troops under Colonel William Henry Clinton landed at Funchal with the reluctant agreement of Britain's oldest ally, to garrison the island against a French or Spanish attack; they left within six months when the Peace of Amiens removed the threat.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Portugal
counterparties.lost: Effective control of one of its Atlantic islands, to an ally it could not refuse. Portuguese sovereignty was never formally challenged, and the Portuguese governor stayed in office.
counterparties.note: The Anglo-Portuguese alliance, in force since the Treaty of Windsor of 1373, is the oldest alliance in the world still in effect, and it is why the occupations were negotiated rather than fought.

acquisitions.how: As Napoleon's army entered Lisbon and the Portuguese royal family fled to Brazil under Royal Navy escort, a British force under General William Carr Beresford occupied Madeira; Beresford at first proclaimed George III its sovereign, and London made him withdraw the claim.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Portugal
counterparties.lost: Seven years of control over the island, though Portuguese law, church and administration continued and Britain governed in the name of the Prince Regent after the first weeks.

people.name: William Carr Beresford
people.role: commanded the 1807 landing, briefly proclaimed British sovereignty, and later reorganised the Portuguese army

contested.note: Accounts differ on how long Beresford's proclamation of British sovereignty stood before it was disavowed, and on the exact date the garrison finally left in 1814.

statusPeriods.label: Garrisoned by an ally
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British garrison held the forts of Funchal; the Portuguese governor kept his office and the island's law, taxes and church were untouched.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default degree of 5 for 'occupied' assumes military government. Britain never displaced the Portuguese administration on Madeira, and after the first weeks of 1808 governed in the Portuguese Prince Regent's name.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Funchal, by the Portuguese governor, with a British garrison commander

statusPeriods.label: Seven years of British garrison
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British troops held the island for the length of the Peninsular War while Portugal's own government was in Rio de Janeiro; the wine trade with Britain boomed and the Portuguese administration continued.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: As in 1801, this was a garrison rather than a government: Portuguese officials, courts and church continued throughout.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Funchal
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain withdrew after the Peace of Amiens in 1802 and returned only when Napoleon invaded Portugal in November 1807.

departures.how: With the Peace of Amiens made and the French threat lifted, the British garrison sailed and left the island entirely to Portugal, having asked for nothing in return.

led.name: William Henry Clinton
led.role: commanded the 1801 garrison and withdrew it

cost.note: No fighting and no recorded deaths from the occupation itself.

departures.borders: None. Madeira remained Portuguese in law throughout, and Britain made no claim on it in 1802.

departures.how: When Napoleon fell, Britain withdrew its garrison and Madeira reverted entirely to Portugal, which had never lost sovereignty over it; the only lasting British legacy was the wine trade and a resident English merchant community.

led.name: William Carr Beresford
led.role: commanded the occupation force in 1807-08 before moving to command the Portuguese army in the Peninsula

led.name: John VI of Portugal
led.role: Prince Regent, then King, whose government in Rio de Janeiro consented to the occupation and received the island back

cost.note: No fighting and no recorded deaths. The occupation was made with Portuguese consent under the alliance of 1373.

departures.borders: None. Madeira went back with the same coastline and the same governor's office.

consequences.economicLegacy: British merchants dominated the Madeira wine trade for two centuries; the fortified wine was shipped in barrels across the Atlantic and back because the heat improved it, and the firms that did it had English names.
consequences.languageAndLaw: No British legal legacy at all: Portuguese law ran throughout both occupations. The Anglican church and the English cemetery in Funchal are the visible remains.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 90,000 to 100,000 people on Madeira in the early nineteenth century, by Portuguese counts; no British census was ever taken.

evidence.author: Desmond Gregory
evidence.work: The Beneficent Usurpers: A History of the British in Madeira
evidence.supports: Both occupations, Beresford's proclamation, and the English merchant community on the island.

evidence.author: Rory Muir
evidence.work: Britain and the Defeat of Napoleon, 1807-1815
evidence.supports: Why Britain occupied Portuguese Atlantic territory in 1807 and the wider Peninsular strategy.

contested.note: The exact dates of arrival and withdrawal in 1801-02 and 1814 are given differently by different accounts, and how far Beresford's brief 1807 proclamation of British sovereignty was ever effective is disputed. The fact of both occupations is not in doubt.

pedagogy.hook: Britain occupied Madeira twice and handed it back both times, and in 1807 a British general proclaimed George III its sovereign before London made him take it back.

misconception.belief: Britain kept everything it occupied.
misconception.correction: Madeira was occupied in 1801 and again from 1807 to 1814, purely to keep it out of French hands and to protect the Portuguese alliance signed in 1373 and still in force. Both times Britain withdrew and asked for nothing. Occupation and annexation are different acts, and the difference usually turned on strategy, not scruple.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Madeira is the counter-example to the idea that British forces never left anywhere voluntarily, and it shows how much of the empire's Atlantic system depended on an alliance rather than on conquest.

keyDates.what: First British occupation of Funchal
Garrison withdrawn after the Peace of Amiens
Second occupation as Napoleon takes Lisbon
Britain withdraws and Madeira reverts to Portugal

territories.name: The Azores
territories.formalName: The Azores: British and later Allied air and naval facilities under Portuguese sovereignty

modernSuccessors.name: Portugal (Autonomous Region of the Azores)
modernSuccessors.note: Portuguese sovereignty was never interrupted. The United States kept the base at Lajes long after Britain left.

to.note: British forces left Lajes during the first half of 1946; the exact departure date is recorded differently in British and Portuguese sources.

geoCoverage.label: Allied airfields on Portuguese soil
geoCoverage.change: Not a colony and never claimed as one: an airfield at Lajes on Terceira and a flying-boat base at Horta, held by agreement with a neutral Portugal.

acquisitions.how: Churchill told the Commons that Britain had invoked the Anglo-Portuguese alliance of 1373 to obtain air and naval facilities in the Azores from neutral Portugal; RAF aircraft flew from Lajes within days and closed the mid-Atlantic gap where U-boats had hunted convoys unobserved.

counterparties.name: The Portuguese Estado Novo under Antonio de Oliveira Salazar
counterparties.lost: Its neutrality in practice, though not in law. Salazar granted the facilities under the terms of the 1373 alliance precisely so that Portugal could remain formally neutral and avoid a German or an Allied invasion.
counterparties.note: Portuguese sovereignty over the islands was explicit in the agreement and was never in question. Nothing here was British territory.

instrument.name: The Anglo-Portuguese agreement of August 1943 on Azores facilities
instrument.note: Made under the Treaty of Windsor of 1373, the oldest alliance still in force; Churchill announced it to Parliament on 12 October 1943.

people.name: Antonio de Oliveira Salazar
people.role: Portuguese dictator who granted the facilities while keeping Portugal formally neutral

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: invoked a 570-year-old alliance in the House of Commons to explain the deal

statusPeriods.label: Allied bases under Portuguese sovereignty
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Portugal governed the islands throughout. Britain, and from November 1944 the United States, ran airfields on them under a written agreement, with no British authority over anybody who was not in uniform.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Angra do Heroismo, by the Portuguese authorities
statusPeriods.note: This record exists because leaving it out makes the empire's reach look smaller than it was. It is drawn at the lowest degree of control precisely because Britain held no sovereignty here at all.

departures.how: Britain's wartime rights at Lajes lapsed after the war and the RAF left in 1946; the United States, admitted to the base in November 1944, negotiated its own agreement with Portugal and stayed for another sixty years.

led.name: Antonio de Oliveira Salazar
led.role: kept sovereignty throughout and rented the base on to the Americans

led.name: Ernest Bevin
led.role: Foreign Secretary whose government ended the British presence and left the Atlantic base to the United States

cost.note: No deaths from the occupation of the airfields; the lives the base saved were in the convoys it covered.

departures.borders: None at any point. Portuguese sovereignty was continuous, and Britain never drew a line or claimed an acre.

consequences.economicLegacy: The wartime airfield at Lajes became the mid-Atlantic staging post for transatlantic aviation and is still a Portuguese air base used by NATO.
consequences.borderLegacy: None: no border was ever drawn, and the episode is in this atlas as an example of reach without sovereignty.

peak.populationNote: About 280,000 Azoreans in the 1940s, none of them under British authority at any point.

evidence.author: Antonio Jose Telo
evidence.work: Portugal na Segunda Guerra (1941-1945)
evidence.supports: The negotiation of the Azores agreement and Portuguese neutrality policy.

evidence.author: Richard Overy
evidence.work: Why the Allies Won
evidence.supports: Why closing the mid-Atlantic air gap mattered to the Battle of the Atlantic in 1943.

contested.note: This is the weakest record in the shard and is marked accordingly. The agreement, the date of Churchill's announcement and the strategic effect are well documented; the exact date the last British personnel left Lajes is not, and Portuguese and British accounts differ. Nothing here was ever British territory.

pedagogy.hook: In 1943 Churchill got Britain an Atlantic airbase by invoking a treaty signed in 1373 — the oldest alliance in the world, and still in force.

misconception.belief: British power abroad always meant British territory.
misconception.correction: Much of the empire's reach was never coloured on any map: treaty ports, coaling stations, base rights and alliances. The Azores were Portuguese throughout, and the airfield Britain flew from there did more against the U-boats in 1943 than several colonies did in a century.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the difference between an empire of territory and an empire of access. When students count only the pink on the map, they miss half of how the system actually worked.

keyDates.what: The Anglo-Portuguese alliance is signed
Portugal agrees to grant the facilities
RAF aircraft begin flying from Lajes
British forces leave; the Americans stay

territories.name: The British Zone of Germany
territories.formalName: The British Zone of Occupation in Germany, administered by the Control Commission for Germany (British Element)

modernSuccessors.name: Germany
modernSuccessors.note: The zone's territory is now the German states of Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia, three of which the British military government created.

geoCoverage.label: North-west Germany, including the Ruhr
geoCoverage.change: Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Lower Saxony and the Ruhr: the most industrial, most bombed and least agricultural of the four occupation zones.

acquisitions.how: The four Allied powers declared on 5 June 1945 that they assumed supreme authority over a Germany that had no government left, and Britain took the north-west: the Ruhr, the ports and 22 million people, governed by a Control Commission that at its peak employed tens of thousands of British staff.

counterparties.name: The German Reich
counterparties.lost: Its existence as a state. There was no German government to surrender to and none to negotiate with; the Allies took sovereignty by declaration.

counterparties.name: The people of the British Zone
counterparties.lost: Food, above all. The zone held the Ruhr and almost no farmland; rations fell to about 1,000 calories a day in the spring of 1946, and Britain, still rationed itself, paid to feed a defeated enemy.
counterparties.note: The cost of feeding the zone, running at tens of millions of pounds a year, was the main reason Britain pushed for the merger with the American zone in 1947.

instrument.name: Declaration Regarding the Defeat of Germany and the Assumption of Supreme Authority

people.name: Sir Brian Robertson
people.role: Military Governor of the British zone, 1947-49, then High Commissioner

people.name: Konrad Adenauer
people.role: Lord Mayor of Cologne, dismissed by a British brigadier in October 1945; founded the CDU and became Chancellor of West Germany in 1949

people.name: Kurt Schumacher
people.role: rebuilt the Social Democratic Party from Hanover in the British zone after ten years in Nazi camps

acquisitions.resistance: There was almost none. The occupation's problems were hunger, refugees and coal, not armed opposition; a feared Nazi guerrilla movement never materialised.

statusPeriods.label: British military government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Military Governor ruled by ordinance through the Control Commission: it licensed newspapers and political parties, ran the coal mines, rebuilt the trade unions, denazified about two million people on paper, and created the German states of Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bad Oeynhausen, then Berlin, under the Foreign Office and the Control Office for Germany and Austria
statusPeriods.franchise: Local elections were held from September 1946, state parliaments from April 1947; the occupying power could still overrule anything they passed.
statusPeriods.note: British officials wrote the press licences that founded Die Welt and Der Spiegel, and put worker representatives on the boards of Ruhr steel firms, which is where German co-determination began.

statusPeriods.label: Occupation rights over a German government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Federal Republic governed itself from Bonn; three Allied High Commissioners kept reserved powers over foreign affairs, disarmament, reparations and the Ruhr industries, and could in theory resume full authority.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: After September 1949 the British ran no German ministries. The Occupation Statute reserved only a short list of powers, so a degree of 5 would misdescribe the last six years entirely.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Allied High Commission at Bonn
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in West German federal elections from August 1949.

departures.how: The zone merged with the American zone in January 1947, became part of the Federal Republic of Germany in May 1949, and Britain's remaining occupation rights ended on 5 May 1955 when the Bonn and Paris conventions came into force and West Germany joined NATO four days later.

led.name: Konrad Adenauer
led.role: first Chancellor of the Federal Republic, who negotiated the end of the occupation regime

led.name: Ernest Bevin
led.role: Foreign Secretary who pushed for a West German state and for the merger of the zones because Britain could not afford the occupation

led.name: Anthony Eden
led.role: Foreign Secretary who rescued the settlement after the European Defence Community collapsed in 1954

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. The cost of the occupation was counted in hunger: the winter of 1946-47 killed an unrecorded number of Germans in the zone through cold and malnutrition, while Britain spent heavily on food it was still rationing at home.

departures.borders: The zone's internal lines became German states that still exist: North Rhine-Westphalia, created by British ordinance in August 1946, is now Germany's most populous Land. The zone's eastern edge became part of the inner German border until 1990.

instrument.name: The Bonn-Paris conventions (General Treaty on relations with the Federal Republic)
instrument.note: Signed in 1952, delayed for three years by the failure of the European Defence Community, and in force on 5 May 1955.

populationTransfer.note: The zone absorbed millions of Germans expelled from the east: Schleswig-Holstein's population rose by more than a third in three years, and the refugees were housed in camps, barns and former barracks.

violence.note: The occupation was not fought against; its violence was the aftermath of the war it followed. British courts in the zone tried the Belsen and Neuengamme cases, and hanged those convicted.

consequences.economicLegacy: British officials restructured the Ruhr coal and steel industries, refounded the trade unions as industry-wide bodies, and placed worker representatives on company boards; German co-determination and the industrial union structure both begin in the British zone.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The press licences issued by the Control Commission created Die Welt, Die Zeit and Der Spiegel, and the BBC's model shaped Nordwestdeutscher Rundfunk, the ancestor of two of Germany's public broadcasters.

peak.populationNote: The October 1946 census counted about 22.3 million people in the British zone, swollen by expellees from the east. It was the most populous of the four zones and the largest population Britain ever administered in Europe.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1946 census of The British Zone of Germany
populationWarrant.supports: The British Zone of Germany’s largest recorded population: 22,300,000 people, counted in 1946.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
