areaWarrant.supports: The British Zone of Germany’s greatest extent, 97,000 km² in 1946: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 98,336 km², within 1.4% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Christopher Knowles
evidence.work: Winning the Peace: The British in Occupied Germany, 1945-1948
evidence.supports: How the Control Commission worked, who staffed it, and what it did and failed to do.

evidence.author: Ian D. Turner
evidence.work: Reconstruction in Post-War Germany: British Occupation Policy and the Western Zones, 1945-55
evidence.supports: Economic policy in the zone, the Ruhr industries, and the road to the Federal Republic.

pedagogy.hook: In October 1945 a British brigadier sacked the Mayor of Cologne for incompetence. The mayor was Konrad Adenauer, who founded a party and became Chancellor of West Germany four years later.

misconception.belief: The British Empire was finished by 1945 and Britain governed nobody new after the war.
misconception.correction: In 1945 Britain took responsibility for about 22 million Germans in the north-west of a wrecked country, running the coal, the ports and the food supply through a Control Commission of tens of thousands of staff. It was the largest population Britain ever governed in Europe, and in law it lasted until 1955.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The German occupation is the clearest case of British rule that nobody calls empire, and comparing it with a colony is the fastest way to see what colonial rule actually consisted of — and what it left out.

keyDates.what: The Allies assume supreme authority over Germany
British ordinance creates North Rhine-Westphalia
British and American zones merge as the Bizone
The Federal Republic of Germany is founded
Occupation ends; West Germany becomes sovereign

events.title: The Plantation of Ulster

date.note: The scheme was drafted in 1609 and the first grants were made in 1610; settlement continued for thirty years, so no single date fits.

events.summary: After the Gaelic earls fled Ulster in September 1607, the Crown confiscated about 500,000 acres in six counties and granted them to English and Scottish settlers, London livery companies and 'deserving' Irish, on condition that the settlers were Protestant and the Irish were moved off the best land.
events.significance: It created the Protestant population of northern Ireland and, three centuries later, the case for partition. It was also the empire's first full colonisation scheme: the same men, the same language of 'planting' and the same investors moved on to Virginia.

places.name: Rathmullan, County Donegal
places.note: Where the earls took ship on 4 September 1607.

places.name: Derry / Londonderry
places.note: Granted to the City of London livery companies in 1613 and renamed for them; the walls they built still stand.

people.name: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone
people.role: left Ireland in the Flight of the Earls, which made the confiscation legally possible

people.name: Sir Arthur Chichester
people.role: Lord Deputy who drove the plantation scheme

people.name: James I and VI
people.role: granted the escheated lands and required the London companies to fund the settlement of Derry

pedagogy.hook: The City of London was made to pay for a colony in Ireland, and renamed a town after itself: Derry became Londonderry in 1613.

misconception.belief: Protestants in Northern Ireland are British settlers who arrived recently, or Catholics there are newcomers.
misconception.correction: The main plantation ran from 1610 and the private Scottish settlement of Antrim and Down began in 1606. The families involved have been in Ulster for over four hundred years — longer than most European settlement in North America. Neither community is new, which is exactly what makes the argument so hard.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Plantation was the technique: confiscate, grant to loyal settlers, exclude the previous owners from the best land, and make religion the test of loyalty. It was tried in Munster in the 1580s, perfected in Ulster after 1609, and carried to Virginia.

evidence.author: Nicholas Canny
evidence.work: Making Ireland British, 1580-1650
evidence.supports: The plantation scheme, who received land, and the link to Atlantic colonisation.

evidence.author: Jonathan Bardon
evidence.work: A History of Ulster
evidence.supports: The settlement of Ulster county by county and the numbers of settlers.

events.title: The Irish Rebellion of 1641
events.summary: Dispossessed Ulster Catholic gentry seized forts and towns in an attempted coup, which broke down into attacks on Protestant settlers in which several thousand were killed and many more stripped and driven out in winter. Reprisals against Catholics followed at once.
events.significance: The massacres, hugely exaggerated in English print, made Ireland a religious cause in England and supplied the justification for Cromwell's reconquest eight years later. They also began twelve years of war that killed a fifth or more of Ireland's population.

places.name: Portadown, County Armagh
places.note: Site of the best-documented massacre, where about a hundred Protestant settlers were drowned in the Bann.

people.name: Sir Phelim O'Neill
people.role: led the rising in Ulster and forged a royal commission to justify it; executed in 1653

people.name: Rory O'More
people.role: one of the planners of the conspiracy in Leinster

toll.note: Modern estimates of settlers killed directly, with many more dying of exposure after being driven from their homes. Contemporary English pamphlets claimed 150,000 or more; the 1641 Depositions in Trinity College Dublin, on which the claims rested, are sworn statements by survivors and are not a body count.

pedagogy.hook: English pamphlets said 150,000 Protestants had been murdered in Ireland. The real figure was a small fraction of that, and the exaggeration did more damage than the truth.

misconception.belief: Death tolls in old sources are roughly accurate because people had no reason to lie.
misconception.correction: They had every reason. The 1641 figures were printed in London to raise money and troops, and the inflated numbers became the moral licence for Cromwell's campaign. Historians now use the same depositions as evidence of both the killings and the propaganda built on them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: 1641 shows how atrocity numbers become political weapons, and it is the point at which Ireland's religious divide became a matter of life and property rather than of doctrine.

evidence.author: Nicholas Canny
evidence.work: Making Ireland British, 1580-1650
evidence.supports: The course of the rising and the use of the 1641 Depositions as evidence.

contested.note: The number killed in 1641 has been argued over for four centuries and is still argued over. What is agreed is that the contemporary figure of 150,000 was propaganda and that several thousand people died.

events.title: Cromwell's Conquest of Ireland
events.summary: Oliver Cromwell landed at Dublin with 12,000 men, stormed Drogheda in September 1649 and Wexford in October, killing the garrisons and many townspeople, and left in May 1650. His subordinates finished a war of sieges, famine and transportation that ended in 1653 with the confiscation of most Catholic-owned land.
events.significance: It is the single most destructive episode in Irish history before the Famine, and it settled the land question for two centuries: Catholic ownership fell from about 60% of the island to under 10%. Cromwell's name is still an insult in Ireland and a hero's in parts of England.

places.name: Drogheda
places.note: Stormed on 11 September 1649; the garrison of about 2,800 was killed, along with priests and an unknown number of townspeople.

places.name: Wexford
places.note: Sacked on 11 October 1649 while surrender terms were still being negotiated; about 2,000 died.

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: commanded the invasion and ordered the storms of Drogheda and Wexford

people.name: Sir Arthur Aston
people.role: royalist governor of Drogheda, beaten to death with his own wooden leg

people.name: Henry Ireton
people.role: Cromwell's son-in-law, who commanded after his departure and died of plague at Limerick in 1651

toll.note: Deaths across the whole war of 1641-53, from fighting, famine and plague. William Petty's contemporary estimate of 616,000 is disputed; modern historians put the population loss at between 15% and 40%. Perhaps 12,000 people were also transported to the Caribbean as indentured labour.

pedagogy.hook: Cromwell was in Ireland for nine months. The land settlement he began took the country's Catholic landowners from owning three fifths of it to owning less than a tenth.

misconception.belief: Irish people shipped to the Caribbean in the 1650s were 'Irish slaves', the same as enslaved Africans.
misconception.correction: Several thousand Irish prisoners and vagrants were transported to Barbados and Montserrat and worked brutally, as indentured servants for a fixed term. Their children were born free. Chattel slavery was lifelong, inheritable and racial in law. The conditions overlapped; the legal categories did not, and the 'Irish slaves' claim is used today mainly to dismiss the history of African enslavement.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Cromwellian settlement is where the Irish land question begins, and every rebellion from 1798 to 1916 argued about it.

evidence.author: Micheal O Siochru
evidence.work: God's Executioner: Oliver Cromwell and the Conquest of Ireland
evidence.supports: The campaign, the storms of Drogheda and Wexford, and the land settlement.

contested.note: Whether the killing of the Drogheda garrison was within the seventeenth-century laws of war, which allowed no quarter to a town that refused to surrender, and how many civilians died there, are both still argued by military historians.

events.title: The Battle of the Boyne

date.note: 1 July by the Julian calendar then used in Britain and Ireland, which is 11 July by the modern calendar. The Twelfth of July commemorations combine the Boyne with the decisive battle of Aughrim, fought on 12 July 1691.

events.summary: William of Orange, with a Dutch, Danish, Huguenot and English army of about 36,000, defeated his father-in-law James II and a Franco-Irish army of about 25,000 at a ford on the River Boyne. James left for France within days; the war went on for another fifteen months.
events.significance: The Boyne decided that Ireland would be governed by a Protestant landowning minority under the Penal Laws, a settlement that lasted until 1829 and shaped everything after it. It is also the most commemorated battle in the British Isles, marched every July in Northern Ireland.

places.name: Oldbridge, County Meath
places.note: The ford where William's army crossed the Boyne.

places.name: Aughrim, County Galway
places.note: The battle of 12 July 1691 that actually decided the war; about 7,000 died there, more than at the Boyne.

people.name: William III of Orange
people.role: commanded the Williamite army; a Dutch prince backed, at the time, by the Pope against Louis XIV

people.name: James II and VII
people.role: commanded the Jacobite army and left Ireland for France after the defeat

people.name: Patrick Sarsfield
people.role: Jacobite cavalry commander who fought on for another year and negotiated the Treaty of Limerick

toll.note: Roughly 1,500 Jacobite and 500 Williamite dead, by the usual estimates; the Boyne was a large battle with unusually few casualties. Aughrim the following year killed about 7,000.

pedagogy.hook: The Battle of the Boyne was fought on 1 July, is commemorated on 12 July, and was welcomed at the time by the Pope, who was at war with Louis XIV.

misconception.belief: The Boyne was a battle between Irish Catholics and English Protestants.
misconception.correction: William's army included Dutch, Danes, Huguenots, Germans and Ulster Protestants; James's included French regiments and Irish Catholics. It was a battle in a European war over the balance of power against Louis XIV, and the Papacy was on William's side.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how a European dynastic war became, in memory, a local sectarian one — and how the memory then became a fact of politics that outlived everything else about it.

evidence.author: Padraig Lenihan
evidence.work: 1690: Battle of the Boyne
evidence.supports: The armies, the course of the battle and the casualty figures.

events.title: The United Irishmen Rebellion
events.summary: The Society of United Irishmen, founded by Protestant and Catholic radicals inspired by America and France, rose in Leinster and Ulster and held most of County Wexford for a month. The army broke the rising at Vinegar Hill on 21 June; a French landing at Killala in August came too late.
events.significance: About 20,000 to 30,000 people died in twelve weeks, more than in any other event in modern Irish history except the Famine. The rising convinced Pitt that Ireland's separate parliament was unsafe, and produced the Act of Union two years later.

places.name: Vinegar Hill, Enniscorthy
places.note: The Wexford rebels' camp, stormed on 21 June 1798.

places.name: Killala, County Mayo
places.note: Where about 1,100 French troops under General Humbert landed on 22 August 1798.

people.name: Theobald Wolfe Tone
people.role: Protestant Dublin barrister who founded the United Irishmen and sought French help; captured in November 1798 and died in prison after cutting his own throat

people.name: Henry Joy McCracken
people.role: Belfast Presbyterian who led the rising in Antrim; hanged in Belfast in July 1798

people.name: Father John Murphy
people.role: priest who led the Wexford rebels after his own bishop condemned them; executed in July 1798

people.name: Charles Cornwallis
people.role: Lord Lieutenant sent to end the killing and then to carry the Union; the same man who had surrendered at Yorktown in 1781

toll.note: Estimates vary widely and include rebels killed in battle, prisoners killed after it, civilians massacred by the United Irishmen and by Crown forces, and reprisal killings. The figure of about 30,000 is the one most often given; some historians argue for a lower total.

pedagogy.hook: The founder of Irish republicanism was an Anglican barrister from Dublin, and the rebellion's fiercest fighters in the north were Presbyterians.

misconception.belief: Irish nationalism has always been a Catholic movement against Protestants.
misconception.correction: The United Irishmen were founded in Belfast in 1791 by Presbyterians and Anglicans who wanted a non-sectarian republic, and Wolfe Tone's aim was to 'substitute the common name of Irishman' for Protestant, Catholic and Dissenter. The rising's defeat, and the sectarian killings inside it, helped destroy that alliance.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: 1798 is the moment Irish politics could have gone another way, and the moment Britain decided that Ireland needed to be governed from Westminster.

evidence.author: Marianne Elliott
evidence.work: Wolfe Tone: Prophet of Irish Independence
evidence.supports: The United Irishmen, the French connection, and Tone's aims and death.

evidence.author: Thomas Bartlett
evidence.work: Ireland: A History
evidence.supports: The course and casualties of the 1798 rising and its consequences for the Union.

contested.note: The death toll and how far the Wexford rising was sectarian rather than republican are both argued. So is whether the rebellion was a genuine mass movement or a conspiracy that collapsed into local violence when its leadership was arrested.

events.title: The Act of Union with Ireland
events.summary: The Irish Parliament voted itself out of existence and Ireland became part of the United Kingdom, sending about 100 MPs and 32 peers to Westminster. The measure was carried in Dublin at the second attempt after the government created peerages and paid over a million pounds in compensation for abolished boroughs.
events.significance: It made Ireland legally part of the metropolitan state rather than a colony, which is why the Famine happened inside the United Kingdom and why partition in 1921 required an Act of Parliament rather than a treaty of independence.

places.name: Parliament House, College Green, Dublin
places.note: The Irish Parliament that abolished itself; the building was sold to the Bank of Ireland in 1803 on condition that the debating chambers be altered beyond use.

people.name: William Pitt the Younger
people.role: Prime Minister who carried the Union and promised Catholic Emancipation with it; resigned in 1801 when George III refused

people.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
people.role: Chief Secretary for Ireland who managed the votes, the peerages and the payments

people.name: Henry Grattan
people.role: leader of the parliamentary opposition to the Union, who had won Ireland's legislative independence in 1782

pedagogy.hook: The Irish Parliament voted itself out of existence in 1800, and the government paid more than a million pounds to the owners of the seats it abolished.

misconception.belief: Ireland was a British colony throughout the nineteenth century.
misconception.correction: From 1801 Ireland was legally part of the United Kingdom, with about 100 MPs at Westminster and no separate government. It was also governed by a Lord Lieutenant in Dublin Castle, policed by an armed national force, and placed under emergency coercion acts dozens of times. Both descriptions are true, which is why the argument is still live.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Union is the reason Ireland's history sits awkwardly in an atlas of empire: it was ruled like a colony and counted as part of the metropolis.

evidence.author: Alvin Jackson
evidence.work: Ireland 1798-1998: Politics and War
evidence.supports: The passage of the Union, the inducements used, and its constitutional consequences.

events.title: Catholic Emancipation
events.summary: Daniel O'Connell won a by-election in County Clare in 1828 that he was legally barred from taking, and mass organisation behind him convinced Wellington's government that refusal risked civil war. The Roman Catholic Relief Act let Catholics sit in Parliament for the first time since 1691.
events.significance: It was the first great victory of organised, disciplined mass politics anywhere in Europe, won by a colonised majority against a government that had said no for thirty years — and it was paid for by an act that stripped the vote from about 85% of Irish county voters in the same session.

places.name: Ennis, County Clare
places.note: Where O'Connell was elected in July 1828 as a Catholic who could not take his seat.

people.name: Daniel O'Connell
people.role: founder of the Catholic Association, elected for Clare in 1828; known as the Liberator

people.name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
people.role: Prime Minister who conceded emancipation against his own convictions to avoid a rising

people.name: Robert Peel
people.role: Home Secretary who had opposed emancipation for years and drafted the Act

pedagogy.hook: The government gave Irish Catholics the right to sit in Parliament and, in the same session, took the vote away from four fifths of the Irish men who had put them there.

misconception.belief: Rights in the empire were granted from above when the time was right.
misconception.correction: The Catholic Association enrolled hundreds of thousands of members at a penny a month, organised through parish priests, and elected a man who could not legally sit. Wellington conceded because his commanders told him Ireland was ungovernable otherwise. Then the franchise qualification was raised from forty shillings to ten pounds, cutting the Irish county electorate by roughly 85%.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: O'Connell invented the modern mass political movement — subscriptions, membership, discipline, a newspaper and a leader — and every later independence movement in the empire used the model.

evidence.author: Paul Bew
evidence.work: Ireland: The Politics of Enmity 1789-2006
evidence.supports: The emancipation campaign, the Clare election and the accompanying disenfranchisement.

events.title: The Great Famine
events.summary: A water mould destroyed the potato crop on which about three million of Ireland's poorest people depended almost entirely. Roughly a million died of starvation and disease and another million emigrated, while grain, butter and livestock continued to be exported from Irish ports, some of it under military escort.
events.significance: Ireland lost a quarter of its people in seven years, inside the United Kingdom, in the richest economy in the world. The famine set the terms of Irish politics and of Irish America for a century, and it is the central exhibit in the argument about what British rule in Ireland actually was.

places.name: Skibbereen, County Cork
places.note: The town whose mass graves were reported in the Illustrated London News in 1847 and became the famine's image.

places.name: Grosse Ile, Quebec
places.note: The quarantine station where thousands of emigrants died of typhus in 1847.

people.name: Charles Trevelyan
people.role: Assistant Secretary to the Treasury who administered relief, closed the food depots in 1847 and wrote that the famine was a judgement of Providence

people.name: Sir Robert Peel
people.role: Prime Minister who bought Indian corn and repealed the Corn Laws in 1846, and lost office for it

people.name: Lord John Russell
people.role: Prime Minister from 1846, whose government shifted the cost of relief onto Irish rate-payers under the Poor Law

people.name: William Smith O'Brien
people.role: led the failed Young Ireland rising of 1848 in protest at the government's response

toll.note: Excess deaths 1846-51 as estimated by Cormac O Grada and Joel Mokyr; emigration from passenger records, which undercount. The census fell from 8,175,124 in 1841 to 6,552,385 in 1851.
toll.source: Cormac O Grada and Joel Mokyr's excess-mortality estimates; the Census of Ireland, 1841 and 1851; passenger records for emigration, which undercount.

pedagogy.hook: Ireland exported food throughout the famine. In 1847, the worst year, ships carrying grain and butter left Irish ports while people died in ditches within sight of the quays.

misconception.belief: The famine was a natural disaster: the potato failed and there was nothing anyone could do.
misconception.correction: The blight was natural; the death toll was not. Relief was cut in 1847 and the cost shifted to bankrupt Irish rate-payers; the Gregory clause denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter of an acre, so families gave up their land to eat; and food kept being exported. Amartya Sen's work on entitlement shows famines are usually about who can buy food, not whether food exists.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the model case for the whole atlas: a catastrophe whose cause was partly natural and whose scale was made by policy, argued over by historians who agree on the facts and disagree on the weighting.

evidence.author: Cormac O Grada
evidence.work: Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory
evidence.supports: Mortality and emigration estimates, and the economics of relief.

evidence.author: Christine Kinealy
evidence.work: This Great Calamity: The Irish Famine 1845-52
evidence.supports: Government relief policy, the food exports, and the Poor Law.

contested.note: Whether the British government's response amounted to negligence, ideological rigidity or something worse is genuinely disputed. The word genocide is used by some writers and rejected by most specialists, who point out that the government did spend and did import food, and then failed catastrophically at scale from 1847.

events.title: The Land War
events.summary: Michael Davitt and Charles Stewart Parnell founded the Irish National Land League in 1879 to fight evictions by rent strikes and by socially isolating land-grabbers. The tactic took its name from Captain Charles Boycott, a Mayo land agent whose workers, shops and postman refused to deal with him in 1880.
events.significance: It broke the power of the Anglo-Irish landlord class through a mass, mostly non-violent campaign, and produced land acts in 1881 and 1903 that eventually transferred most Irish farmland to its tenants. It also gave the English language the word boycott and gave later anti-colonial movements a tested tactic.

places.name: Lough Mask House, County Mayo
places.note: Charles Boycott's house, where the tactic that took his name was first used in the autumn of 1880.

people.name: Michael Davitt
people.role: founder of the Land League; son of evicted tenants, lost an arm in a Lancashire mill at eleven, and spent seven years in English prisons

people.name: Charles Stewart Parnell
people.role: Protestant landlord who led the Irish Parliamentary Party and the Land League and coined the boycott tactic in a speech at Ennis

people.name: Anna Parnell
people.role: organised the Ladies' Land League, which ran the campaign while the male leaders were in prison and was then shut down by them

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: Prime Minister who jailed Parnell and then legislated for the tenants

pedagogy.hook: The word boycott is the name of a Mayo land agent whose neighbours in 1880 simply stopped speaking to him, working for him, or selling him bread.

misconception.belief: Colonised people could only resist by fighting or by petitioning.
misconception.correction: The Land League showed a third way: mass, disciplined, economic non-cooperation. It was studied and copied — Gandhi cited the Irish example, and boycotts of goods and officials became a standard anti-colonial weapon from India to the American civil rights movement.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in the empire of a mass movement changing property law in the metropolitan parliament without winning a single election in it.

evidence.author: Paul Bew
evidence.work: Land and the National Question in Ireland, 1858-82
evidence.supports: The Land League, the boycott campaign and the 1881 Land Act.

events.title: The Home Rule Crisis
events.summary: The third Home Rule Bill promised Ireland a parliament in Dublin. Ulster unionists answered with a Covenant signed by 471,000 people and a private army that landed 25,000 German rifles at Larne; nationalists armed in reply, and British officers at the Curragh said they would resign rather than coerce Ulster.
events.significance: Two private armies and a mutinous officer corps made partition thinkable before a shot had been fired in anger. The Act reached the statute book in September 1914 and was suspended for the duration of the war, and by the time the war ended the political ground had gone.

places.name: Belfast City Hall
places.note: Where Edward Carson signed the Ulster Covenant on 28 September 1912.

places.name: Larne, County Antrim
places.note: Where the UVF landed about 25,000 rifles from Germany on 24-25 April 1914 without interference.

people.name: Edward Carson
people.role: Dublin-born barrister who led Ulster unionism and organised armed resistance to a law of the United Kingdom

people.name: James Craig
people.role: organised the Covenant and the UVF, and became Northern Ireland's first Prime Minister

people.name: John Redmond
people.role: leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, who won Home Rule on paper and lost his party by backing the war

people.name: H. H. Asquith
people.role: Prime Minister whose government could neither enforce its own Act nor abandon it

pedagogy.hook: In 1914 a private army in Ulster imported 25,000 German rifles to stop a British Act of Parliament, and no one was prosecuted.

misconception.belief: Partition was a British idea imposed on Ireland in 1921.
misconception.correction: The demand for exclusion came from Ulster unionists from 1912, was conceded in principle by Asquith's government in 1914, and was legislated in the Government of Ireland Act 1920 before the Treaty was signed. Britain drew the line; the demand for a line came from within Ireland.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The crisis shows the moment when constitutional nationalism stopped working: if an armed minority could veto an Act of Parliament, then the argument for physical force was being made by unionists as much as by republicans.

evidence.author: Alvin Jackson
evidence.work: Home Rule: An Irish History 1800-2000
evidence.supports: The Home Rule bills, the Ulster Covenant, the gun-running and the road to partition.

events.title: The Easter Rising
events.summary: About 1,500 members of the Irish Volunteers and the Irish Citizen Army seized buildings in Dublin on Easter Monday and proclaimed a republic from the General Post Office. British artillery reduced the centre of the city and the rebels surrendered after six days; most Dubliners jeered them as they were marched away.
events.significance: The rising failed militarily and was unpopular. What changed Ireland was the response: fifteen leaders were shot in Kilmainham Gaol between 3 and 12 May, one of them tied to a chair because he could not stand. Within two years Sinn Fein had replaced the constitutional nationalists entirely.

places.name: The General Post Office, Sackville Street, Dublin
places.note: Rebel headquarters, where the Proclamation of the Republic was read on Easter Monday.

places.name: Kilmainham Gaol, Dublin
places.note: Where fourteen of the leaders were shot between 3 and 12 May 1916.

people.name: Patrick Pearse
people.role: teacher and poet who read the Proclamation and commanded the rising; shot on 3 May

people.name: James Connolly
people.role: socialist and trade union leader who commanded the Citizen Army; too badly wounded to stand, he was shot tied to a chair on 12 May

people.name: Constance Markievicz
people.role: second in command at St Stephen's Green; her death sentence was commuted because she was a woman, which she protested

people.name: Elizabeth O'Farrell
people.role: nurse and Cumann na mBan member who carried the surrender through the fighting under a white flag

people.name: General John Maxwell
people.role: commanded the British response and ordered the executions by secret court martial

toll.note: Research for the 2016 centenary counted 485 deaths: about 260 civilians, 143 British soldiers and police, and 82 rebels. Forty of the dead were children. Sixteen leaders were executed afterwards, including Roger Casement, hanged in London in August.

pedagogy.hook: More civilians than rebels died in the Easter Rising, and Dubliners threw rotten vegetables at the prisoners. Two weeks of executions turned those prisoners into founders.

misconception.belief: The Easter Rising was a popular uprising that won Irish independence.
misconception.correction: It lasted six days, involved about 1,500 people, and was widely condemned in Dublin, where most of the 485 dead were civilians killed by artillery and crossfire. It changed everything because of what followed: fifteen secret courts martial and executions in nine days, then mass internment, then a general election in 1918 that Sinn Fein won by a landslide.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest example in the empire of repression creating the movement it was meant to destroy — a pattern British governments repeated in India in 1919 and in Cyprus and Kenya in the 1950s.

evidence.author: Charles Townshend
evidence.work: Easter 1916: The Irish Rebellion
evidence.supports: The planning, the six days of fighting, the casualties and the executions.

evidence.author: Diarmaid Ferriter
evidence.work: The Transformation of Ireland 1900-2000
evidence.supports: Public reaction to the rising and the political collapse of constitutional nationalism after it.

events.title: The Irish War of Independence
events.summary: On the day the First Dail met in Dublin, Volunteers killed two policemen at Soloheadbeg. Two and a half years of ambushes and raids followed, met by police reinforced with British ex-servicemen, the Black and Tans and the Auxiliaries, who burned creameries, sacked Cork and fired into a crowd at Croke Park.
events.significance: It was the first successful war of independence against Britain in the twentieth century and the template for later ones: a shadow government collecting taxes and running courts, a guerrilla force that avoided battle, and a British public that would not stomach the reprisals needed to win.

places.name: Soloheadbeg, County Tipperary
places.note: The ambush of 21 January 1919 conventionally taken as the war's first action.

places.name: Croke Park, Dublin
places.note: Where police and Auxiliaries fired into a crowd at a Gaelic football match on 21 November 1920, killing fourteen.

places.name: Kilmichael, County Cork
places.note: Where Tom Barry's flying column killed seventeen Auxiliaries on 28 November 1920.

people.name: Michael Collins
people.role: director of intelligence, who ran a network inside Dublin Castle and a squad that killed British agents

people.name: Tom Barry
people.role: commanded the West Cork flying column at Kilmichael and Crossbarry

people.name: Cathal Brugha
people.role: Minister for Defence in the underground Dail government

people.name: Terence MacSwiney
people.role: Lord Mayor of Cork who died on hunger strike in Brixton Prison after 74 days, an event reported around the world

people.name: Hamar Greenwood
people.role: Chief Secretary for Ireland who defended the reprisals in the House of Commons

toll.note: About 1,400 people died to the truce of July 1921 by Charles Townshend's count: roughly 550 police and soldiers, 400 IRA members and 750 civilians, though the categories overlap and republican and British counts differ.

pedagogy.hook: On 21 November 1920 Michael Collins's squad killed fourteen British agents in their beds before breakfast. That afternoon police fired into a football crowd at Croke Park and killed fourteen people.

misconception.belief: The Black and Tans were a separate army sent to terrorise Ireland.
misconception.correction: They were British ex-servicemen recruited into the Royal Irish Constabulary from January 1920 because Irish recruitment had collapsed, and the Auxiliaries were a separate corps of ex-officers. Both were police, which is why their reprisals were so shocking, and why the government spent 1920 denying that reprisals were happening.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the war that taught the empire its own weakness: a small guerrilla force with popular support and a functioning shadow state could make a country ungovernable at a cost Britain would not pay.

evidence.author: Charles Townshend
evidence.work: The Republic: The Fight for Irish Independence, 1918-1923
evidence.supports: The course of the war, the counter-insurgency and the casualty figures.

events.title: The Anglo-Irish Treaty
events.summary: After two months of negotiation in London, the Irish delegates signed a treaty giving 26 counties dominion status as the Irish Free State, with an oath to the Crown, three naval bases retained by Britain, and the six counties of Northern Ireland free to opt out, which they did immediately.
events.significance: It ended British rule over most of Ireland and split the movement that had won it. The Dail approved the treaty by 64 votes to 57 on 7 January 1922, and the two sides of that vote became the two main parties of the Irish state and fought a civil war first.

places.name: 10 Downing Street, London
places.note: Where the treaty was signed at about 2.20 in the morning of 6 December 1921.

people.name: Arthur Griffith
people.role: led the Irish delegation and defended the treaty as the most that could be got

people.name: Michael Collins
people.role: signed, saying he had signed his own death warrant; he was killed eight months later

people.name: Eamon de Valera
people.role: President of the Dail, who stayed in Dublin, rejected the treaty and led the walkout

people.name: David Lloyd George
people.role: Prime Minister who ended the negotiation by threatening 'immediate and terrible war' within three days

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: Colonial Secretary and treaty negotiator, who then pressed the new government to attack the anti-treaty garrison in Dublin

pedagogy.hook: Michael Collins signed the treaty at 2.20 in the morning and wrote that he had signed his own death warrant. He was shot in an ambush in his own county eight months later.

misconception.belief: The split over the treaty was about partition.
misconception.correction: Partition was barely debated in the Dail treaty debates. The argument was about the oath of allegiance to the Crown and dominion status rather than a republic. Pro-Treaty and anti-Treaty deputies alike assumed a promised Boundary Commission would make Northern Ireland unviable; it reported in 1925 and its report was suppressed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The treaty is the model for how Britain left an empire: a negotiated settlement, under threat of force, with a partition attached and a promise about the border that was never kept.

evidence.author: Charles Townshend
evidence.work: The Republic: The Fight for Irish Independence, 1918-1923
evidence.supports: The negotiations, the terms, and the Dail debates and vote.

contested.note: Whether Lloyd George's threat of immediate war was real or a bluff, and whether the delegates had authority to sign without referring back to Dublin, are still argued and were the central charges in the Dail debates.

events.title: The Irish Civil War
events.summary: The Free State government, pressed by London and using British artillery, shelled the anti-treaty garrison holding the Four Courts in Dublin. Eleven months of fighting followed between former comrades; the Free State executed 77 republican prisoners, more than the British had executed in the previous war.
events.significance: It secured the new state and poisoned its politics for eighty years. The two sides became Cumann na nGaedheal and Fianna Fail, the parties that have governed Ireland ever since, and the memory of the executions shaped Irish attitudes to political violence for generations.

places.name: The Four Courts, Dublin
places.note: Shelled from 28 June 1922; the Public Record Office beside it burned, destroying seven centuries of Irish archives.

places.name: Beal na Blath, County Cork
places.note: Where Michael Collins was killed in an ambush on 22 August 1922.

people.name: Michael Collins
people.role: commanded the Free State army until he was killed in an ambush in County Cork

people.name: Liam Lynch
people.role: chief of staff of the anti-treaty IRA, killed in the Knockmealdown mountains in April 1923

people.name: W. T. Cosgrave
people.role: led the Free State government that carried out the executions

people.name: Kevin O'Higgins
people.role: Minister for Home Affairs who authorised the execution policy, including that of his own best man; assassinated in 1927

toll.note: No agreed figure exists; Michael Hopkinson gives a range and notes that record-keeping was worst in the civil war. Seventy-seven republican prisoners were executed by the Free State, and about 12,000 were interned.

pedagogy.hook: The Irish Free State executed 77 republican prisoners in ten months. The British had executed 24 in the entire War of Independence.

misconception.belief: Independence ended the violence.
misconception.correction: In Ireland it started a worse one. The civil war killed more people than the War of Independence by some counts, destroyed the national archives in the Four Courts fire, and left a legacy of bitterness that shaped Irish politics until the twenty-first century.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the warning attached to every negotiated independence in this atlas: the settlement Britain offers can become the thing the independence movement fights itself over.

evidence.author: Michael Hopkinson
evidence.work: Green Against Green: The Irish Civil War
evidence.supports: The course of the war, the executions and the difficulty of counting the dead.

contested.note: The civil war's death toll is the worst-recorded figure in modern Irish history. Estimates range from about 1,000 to 4,000 and no reliable count was ever made.

events.title: Ireland Leaves the Commonwealth
events.summary: The Republic of Ireland Act came into force on Easter Monday 1949, declaring the state a republic and ending the last formal link with the Crown. Britain responded with the Ireland Act 1949, which guaranteed that Northern Ireland would remain in the United Kingdom unless its own parliament agreed otherwise.
events.significance: It separates two things students usually merge: leaving the empire and leaving the Commonwealth. Ireland left British rule in 1922 and the Commonwealth in 1949, and the British Act that answered it wrote the unionist veto into law for the next fifty years.

places.name: Leinster House, Dublin
places.note: Seat of the Oireachtas, which passed the Act in 1948.

people.name: John A. Costello
people.role: Taoiseach who announced the repeal of the External Relations Act while on a visit to Canada in September 1948

people.name: Eamon de Valera
people.role: in opposition by then, having built the 1937 constitution that had already left the state a republic in all but name

people.name: Clement Attlee
people.role: Prime Minister whose government answered with the guarantee to Northern Ireland in the Ireland Act 1949

pedagogy.hook: Ireland left the British Empire in 1922 and the Commonwealth in 1949. Twenty-seven years separate the two, and they are not the same event.

misconception.belief: Leaving the empire and leaving the Commonwealth are the same thing.
misconception.correction: India became independent in 1947 and stayed in the Commonwealth as a republic in 1949, which is why the Commonwealth still exists. Ireland became independent in 1922 as a dominion and left the Commonwealth in 1949. Membership was, and is, a separate choice from independence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The London Declaration of April 1949, made for India in the same month Ireland left, invented the modern Commonwealth; Ireland is the state that took the other road.

evidence.author: Diarmaid Ferriter
evidence.work: The Transformation of Ireland 1900-2000
evidence.supports: The 1948 declaration, the 1949 Act and the British response.

events.title: The Troubles

date.note: There is no agreed start date. This atlas uses the police attack on a civil rights march in Derry, which was filmed and broadcast; others date it from August 1969 or from 1966.

events.summary: A civil rights movement demanding an end to discrimination in housing, jobs and local government voting was met with police batons. Loyalist and republican paramilitaries formed, British troops were deployed in August 1969, internment without trial began in 1971, and thirty years of killing followed.
events.significance: About 3,500 people were killed in a region of one and a half million, more than half of them civilians. It was the longest deployment in British Army history and the only sustained armed conflict inside the United Kingdom since the seventeenth century.

places.name: Derry / Londonderry
places.note: Where the civil rights march was attacked in October 1968 and where paratroopers shot dead thirteen unarmed people on 30 January 1972.

places.name: Long Kesh / the Maze, County Down
places.note: Internment camp and then prison; ten republican prisoners died on hunger strike there in 1981.

places.name: Dublin, Talbot Street
places.note: One of the sites of the loyalist car bombings of 17 May 1974 that killed 33 people and an unborn child, the deadliest day of the conflict.

people.name: Bernadette Devlin
people.role: civil rights leader elected to Westminster at 21, the youngest woman MP of her time

people.name: John Hume
people.role: founder of the SDLP, who argued for thirty years that the answer was agreement and not victory; shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize

people.name: Ian Paisley
people.role: preacher and politician who opposed every concession to nationalism, and finally shared power with Sinn Fein in 2007

people.name: Bobby Sands
people.role: IRA prisoner elected to Parliament while on hunger strike; died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days

people.name: Gerry Adams
people.role: Sinn Fein leader whose move to negotiation was central to the 1994 ceasefire

toll.note: The standard count, from the Sutton database and from the book Lost Lives, is about 3,530 dead: roughly 60% killed by republican paramilitaries, 30% by loyalist paramilitaries and 10% by the security forces. More than half of all those killed were civilians. Around 47,000 people were injured.

pedagogy.hook: The British Army was sent to Northern Ireland in August 1969 to protect Catholic areas from loyalist attacks. Within three years it had shot dead thirteen unarmed civil rights marchers in Derry.

misconception.belief: The Troubles were an ancient religious war between Catholics and Protestants.
misconception.correction: The conflict began over civil rights: housing allocation, job discrimination, and a local government franchise that gave extra votes to property owners and drew ward boundaries so that a nationalist majority in Derry elected a unionist council. Religion marked the two communities; the argument was about power, and about whether the state should exist.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the empire's last war inside the United Kingdom, fought over a border drawn in 1921, and it ended by agreement rather than by victory — which is why the agreement is studied by peace negotiators everywhere.

evidence.author: David McKittrick and David McVea
evidence.work: Making Sense of the Troubles
evidence.supports: The narrative of the conflict and the casualty statistics.

evidence.author: David McKittrick, Seamus Kelters, Brian Feeney and Chris Thornton
evidence.work: Lost Lives: The Stories of the Men, Women and Children who Died as a Result of the Northern Ireland Troubles
evidence.supports: The individual record of every death in the conflict, which is the basis for the standard totals.

contested.note: Almost everything about the conflict is contested, including its start date, its name, whether it was a war or a criminal conspiracy, and the extent of collusion between the security forces and loyalist paramilitaries, which several official inquiries have found in specific cases.

events.title: The Good Friday Agreement
events.summary: After two years of talks chaired by the American senator George Mitchell, the British and Irish governments and most of Northern Ireland's parties agreed a settlement: power-sharing at Stormont, cross-border bodies, prisoner releases, police reform, and a status that can change only by consent north and south.
events.significance: It ended thirty years of armed conflict, and it did it by making the constitutional question answerable rather than by answering it. Ireland removed its territorial claim to the north from its constitution, and Britain accepted that Northern Ireland can leave if its people vote to.

places.name: Castle Buildings, Stormont, Belfast
places.note: Where the talks concluded on Good Friday, 10 April 1998.

people.name: John Hume
people.role: SDLP leader whose long argument for consent and partnership underlies the agreement; Nobel Peace Prize 1998

people.name: David Trimble
people.role: Ulster Unionist leader who took the risk of signing and lost his party's leadership over it; Nobel Peace Prize 1998

people.name: George Mitchell
people.role: American senator who chaired the talks

people.name: Mo Mowlam
people.role: Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, who went into the Maze prison to persuade loyalist prisoners to back the talks

people.name: Bertie Ahern
people.role: Taoiseach who agreed to remove the Irish constitution's territorial claim to Northern Ireland

pedagogy.hook: On 22 May 1998 the whole island voted on the same day: 71% yes in Northern Ireland, 94% yes in the Republic, which also voted to delete its own claim to the six counties.

misconception.belief: The Good Friday Agreement settled the border question.
misconception.correction: It did the opposite, deliberately. It set out how the question can be asked and answered in future — by referendums north and south, if the Secretary of State judges a majority likely — and let both communities keep their aims. People in Northern Ireland may hold Irish or British citizenship or both.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the only case in this atlas of a border drawn by empire being made negotiable rather than fought over, and Brexit put it under strain within twenty years.

evidence.author: David McKittrick and David McVea
evidence.work: Making Sense of the Troubles
evidence.supports: The peace process, the negotiations and the referendum results.

events.title: The Union of England and Scotland
events.summary: The Scottish and English parliaments each ratified a Treaty of Union and dissolved themselves into a single parliament at Westminster. Scotland kept its own law, church and universities, gained free trade with England's colonies, and received £398,085 to settle the debts of its failed colony at Darien.
events.significance: It created the state that built the empire. Within a generation Scots were a large and growing share of the empire's soldiers, surgeons, merchants, planters and administrators, out of all proportion to Scotland's tenth of the population.

places.name: Parliament Hall, Edinburgh
places.note: Where the Scottish parliament voted itself out of existence on 25 March 1707.

people.name: Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun
people.role: led the opposition to the Union in the Scottish parliament

people.name: James Douglas, 2nd Duke of Queensberry
people.role: the Queen's Commissioner, who managed the votes

people.name: Daniel Defoe
people.role: sent to Edinburgh as an English government agent to argue and report on Scottish opinion

pedagogy.hook: Scotland's parliament voted itself out of existence in 1707, seven years after Scotland's own attempt at a colony, at Darien in Panama, had swallowed perhaps a quarter of the country's liquid capital.

misconception.belief: Scotland was colonised by England.
misconception.correction: Scotland was not conquered in 1707: its parliament voted for the Union, under heavy pressure and after the Darien disaster, and kept its own legal system, church and universities. Scots then supplied a share of the empire's governors, soldiers, doctors and planters far above their share of Britain's population. The Highlands after 1746 were another matter.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Understanding the Union stops students treating 'Britain' as a single actor with a single motive, and explains why Scottish and Irish people appear on either side of almost every page of this atlas.

evidence.author: Christopher A. Whatley
evidence.work: The Scots and the Union
evidence.supports: The Union debates, the Equivalent payment and Scottish opinion.

evidence.author: T. M. Devine
evidence.work: Scotland's Empire, 1600-1815
evidence.supports: Darien, and the Scottish role in the empire after 1707.

events.title: The Treaty of Utrecht

date.note: The first Utrecht treaties were signed on 11 April 1713; the Anglo-Spanish treaty containing the Gibraltar and Minorca articles was signed on 13 July 1713.

events.summary: The peace that ended the War of the Spanish Succession gave Britain Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Acadia and the Hudson Bay territories, and the asiento: a thirty-year monopoly contract to carry enslaved Africans to Spanish America, granted to the South Sea Company.
events.significance: Utrecht is where Britain becomes a global power on paper. It got two Mediterranean bases, the fisheries and fur of northern North America, and legal entry into the Spanish slave trade — the three things the eighteenth-century empire was built on.

places.name: Utrecht
places.note: Where the treaties were negotiated and signed.

people.name: Henry St John, Viscount Bolingbroke
people.role: Secretary of State who negotiated the peace, and the asiento, in secret with France

people.name: Philip V of Spain
people.role: kept the Spanish throne and lost Gibraltar, Minorca and the Netherlands

pedagogy.hook: In the same treaty that gave Britain Gibraltar, Britain won the right to ship 4,800 enslaved Africans a year to Spanish America for thirty years, and treated it as the greatest prize of the peace.

misconception.belief: Britain's empire was built by explorers and settlers moving into empty land.
misconception.correction: Much of it was won at European conference tables. Utrecht handed Britain Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Acadia and Hudson Bay, and the asiento contract in enslaved people, in a bargain between European monarchs about a Spanish throne. Nobody in Acadia or West Africa was consulted.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single treaty that best shows how the eighteenth-century empire was assembled: bases, fisheries and the slave trade, all taken by diplomacy after a European war.

evidence.author: Hugh Thomas
evidence.work: The Slave Trade: The History of the Atlantic Slave Trade 1440-1870
evidence.supports: The asiento contract granted at Utrecht and what the South Sea Company did with it.

evidence.author: N. A. M. Rodger
evidence.work: The Command of the Ocean: A Naval History of Britain, 1649-1815
evidence.supports: The strategic value of Gibraltar and Minorca and the naval terms of the peace.

events.title: Hanover: a shared king, not an empire
events.summary: When Queen Anne died in 1714 the crown passed to George, Elector of Hanover, and for 123 years the same man was King of Great Britain and ruler of a German state. Hanover kept its own government, army, law and treasury; the union ended in 1837 because Hanoverian law barred a woman from the throne.
events.significance: This is the clearest test case for what empire is and is not. Britain and Hanover shared a monarch and nothing else: no British parliament legislated for Hanover, no British official governed it, and no Hanoverian revenue reached London. A shared head of state is not rule.

places.name: Hanover
places.note: Capital of the Electorate, later Kingdom, of Hanover: never British territory at any point.

people.name: George I
people.role: Elector of Hanover who became King of Great Britain in 1714 and spent much of his reign in Germany

people.name: Queen Victoria
people.role: her accession ended the union in 1837 because Hanoverian succession law excluded women

people.name: Ernest Augustus, Duke of Cumberland
people.role: Victoria's uncle, who took the Hanoverian throne in 1837 and suspended its constitution within months

pedagogy.hook: For 123 years the King of Great Britain also ruled a German state — and it was never part of the British Empire, not for one day.

misconception.belief: Anywhere ruled by the British monarch was part of the British Empire.
misconception.correction: Hanover shared a king with Britain from 1714 to 1837 and was never British: it had its own government, army, law and taxes, and Westminster never legislated for it. The same logic works in reverse today — Canada and Australia share a head of state with Britain and are fully independent states. Sovereignty is about who makes the law, not whose face is on the coins.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Getting Hanover right is how a student learns to read the pink map properly: colour on a map can mean conquest, a lease, a protectorate, a shared monarch, or nothing much at all.

evidence.author: Nick Harding
evidence.work: Hanover and the British Empire, 1700-1837
evidence.supports: The constitutional separation of Britain and Hanover and the arguments about it at the time.

evidence.author: Brendan Simms
evidence.work: Three Victories and a Defeat: The Rise and Fall of the First British Empire
evidence.supports: How Hanover shaped British foreign policy without being British territory.

events.title: English Tangier
events.summary: Tangier came to Charles II in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry, with Bombay and a large cash payment. England garrisoned it for 22 years, built a huge stone mole to make a harbour, fought the forces of Sultan Moulay Ismail outside its walls, and then blew the whole thing up and sailed away.
events.significance: Tangier was England's first African possession, its most expensive military commitment of the century, and its first outright abandonment. Parliament refused to keep paying for a garrison it suspected of being a standing army for a Catholic king, so the empire's earliest Mediterranean base was demolished by its own engineers.

places.name: Tangier
places.note: English from 1661 to 1684. No geo unit exists for it in this atlas, so it is shown as a point.

people.name: Catherine of Braganza
people.role: Portuguese princess whose marriage treaty brought Tangier and Bombay to the English crown

people.name: Moulay Ismail
people.role: Sultan of Morocco whose forces besieged the town for years and reoccupied it in 1684

people.name: Samuel Pepys
people.role: naval administrator who sailed with the evacuation fleet in 1683 and kept a diary of the demolition

people.name: George Legge, Lord Dartmouth
people.role: commanded the 1683-84 evacuation and the destruction of the mole

toll.note: Hundreds of the garrison died in the fighting of 1664 and 1680 and many more from disease; no reliable total was kept. The whole venture is usually reckoned to have cost the Crown around two million pounds.

pedagogy.hook: England's first African colony came with a royal bride, cost about two million pounds, and was blown up by its own engineers in 1684 so that nobody else could use it.

misconception.belief: Britain never gave up territory it had taken.
misconception.correction: It abandoned Tangier in 1684 and destroyed the harbour works on the way out, because Parliament would not fund the garrison and suspected Charles II of using it to keep a standing army out of sight. The empire gave things up whenever they cost more than they earned.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tangier is the empire before it worked: an expensive, badly chosen base held for prestige, abandoned when the money ran out, and almost entirely forgotten.

evidence.author: Linda Colley
evidence.work: Captives: Britain, Empire and the World, 1600-1850
evidence.supports: The Tangier garrison, its cost, and the experience of English captives in Morocco.

evidence.author: E. M. G. Routh
evidence.work: Tangier: England's Lost Atlantic Outpost, 1661-1684
evidence.supports: The detailed narrative of the occupation, the mole and the evacuation.

events.title: The Sale of Dunkirk
events.summary: Cromwell's army had won Dunkirk from Spain at the Battle of the Dunes in 1658, and England held it for four years. In 1662 Charles II sold the port to Louis XIV for about five million livres, roughly £320,000, because the garrison was costing more than the Crown could raise.
events.significance: It is the only time Britain has sold a European possession for cash, and it was hugely unpopular: the Earl of Clarendon, who negotiated it, was still being attacked over Dunkirk when he was impeached five years later. It also shows how thin the line between conquest and account-keeping was.

places.name: Dunkirk
places.note: English from 1658 to 1662. No geo unit exists for it in this atlas, so it is shown as a point.

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: won Dunkirk for England by allying with France against Spain; he died three months later

people.name: Charles II
people.role: sold it four years later to pay his debts

people.name: Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon
people.role: negotiated the sale and was blamed for it for the rest of his career; his London house was nicknamed Dunkirk House

people.name: Louis XIV
people.role: bought the port and had Vauban fortify it as a base for privateers against English shipping

pedagogy.hook: England once owned Dunkirk, and sold it to France in 1662 for about £320,000 because the garrison cost too much.

misconception.belief: Empires only ever expand until they are defeated.
misconception.correction: Territories were traded, sold and abandoned throughout. England sold Dunkirk in 1662, abandoned Tangier in 1684, handed Minorca back in 1802, gave the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864 and swapped Heligoland for Zanzibar in 1890. Empire was a portfolio, and things were sold when they stopped paying.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Dunkirk is the cheapest possible lesson in what territory was actually for: the Crown gave up a fortified port on the Channel because the annual bill was larger than the strategic value.

evidence.author: Ronald Hutton
evidence.work: Charles II: King of England, Scotland, and Ireland
evidence.supports: The decision to sell Dunkirk, the price, and the political damage it caused.

contested.note: The sale price is given in contemporary sources as five million livres and converted variously to between £320,000 and £400,000; exchange rates of the period make any single sterling figure approximate.

events.title: Minorca Lost: the Shooting of Admiral Byng
events.summary: A French force landed on Minorca in April 1756 and besieged Fort St Philip. Admiral John Byng fought an inconclusive action off the island on 20 May, judged he could not relieve the fort and withdrew to Gibraltar. The garrison surrendered; Byng was court-martialled and shot on his own quarterdeck.
events.significance: The loss of Minorca began the Seven Years War badly for Britain and brought down a government. The execution of an admiral for a failure of judgement, not cowardice, made the Royal Navy's officers famously aggressive for a century and gave Voltaire the line about killing an admiral now and then to encourage the others.

places.name: Fort St Philip, Port Mahon
places.note: Besieged from April to June 1756; Spain demolished it after 1782.

places.name: Portsmouth Harbour
places.note: Where Byng was shot by a firing party of marines on the quarterdeck of HMS Monarch.

people.name: John Byng
people.role: admiral executed for failing to relieve Minorca; he refused a blindfold and dropped his own handkerchief as the signal

people.name: William Blakeney
people.role: 84-year-old Lieutenant Governor who held Fort St Philip for ten weeks and was rewarded with a peerage

people.name: Voltaire
people.role: wrote in Candide two years later that in England it is thought good to kill an admiral from time to time to encourage the others

pedagogy.hook: Britain shot an admiral for losing an island. He was not accused of cowardice or treason, only of not doing his utmost.

misconception.belief: Britain's naval dominance came from better ships and better technology.
misconception.correction: It came at least as much from a culture of forced aggression. After Byng, no British admiral could afford to be cautious: the Articles of War made failing to do one's utmost a capital offence, and everyone had seen it enforced. That produced Nelson's tactics, and also produced avoidable disasters.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest example of how the empire was held together by fear as well as by ambition, and of what happened when a government needed someone to blame.

evidence.author: N. A. M. Rodger
evidence.work: The Command of the Ocean: A Naval History of Britain, 1649-1815
evidence.supports: The Minorca campaign, the court martial and its effect on the navy.

evidence.author: Brian Tunstall
evidence.work: Admiral Byng and the Loss of Minorca
evidence.supports: The detailed course of the action off Minorca and the trial.

events.title: The Great Siege of Gibraltar
events.summary: Spain and France besieged Gibraltar for three years and seven months while Britain was losing the American war. The garrison under George Augustus Eliott lived on convoys fought through the blockade, tunnelled galleries into the Rock, and destroyed the Franco-Spanish floating batteries with red-hot shot.
events.significance: It is the longest siege in British military history, and its outcome shaped the peace: Britain lost thirteen colonies in 1783 but kept Gibraltar, and the refusal to trade the Rock away in the negotiations set the pattern for the next 240 years.

places.name: The Rock of Gibraltar
places.note: The garrison tunnelled the Upper Galleries into the north face to fire down on the besiegers; the tunnels are still there.

people.name: George Augustus Eliott
people.role: Governor who commanded the defence for three and a half years

people.name: Luis de Cordova
people.role: commanded the Spanish blockading fleet

people.name: Richard Howe
people.role: fought the last relief convoy through in October 1782

toll.note: Roughly 1,200 of the garrison and civilians died, many of scurvy and smallpox rather than enemy fire; Franco-Spanish losses, including some 2,000 in the destruction of the floating batteries, are less certainly counted. Totals vary widely between British and Spanish accounts.

pedagogy.hook: Britain lost America and kept a rock. In the peace talks of 1782 the cabinet considered trading Gibraltar away and decided the public would not stand for it.

misconception.belief: Losing the American colonies in 1783 broke the British Empire.
misconception.correction: The empire was bigger and richer in 1820 than in 1770. Britain came out of the American war having lost thirteen colonies and held Gibraltar, Canada, the Caribbean sugar islands and a rapidly expanding Company state in India. The centre of the empire moved east; it did not disappear.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The siege is why Gibraltar is still British, and why it became a symbol out of all proportion to its two square miles.

evidence.author: Roy Adkins and Lesley Adkins
evidence.work: Gibraltar: The Greatest Siege in British History
evidence.supports: The course of the siege, the conditions in the garrison and the floating batteries.

events.title: Britain Gives the Ionian Islands to Greece
events.summary: By the Treaty of London of March 1864 Britain transferred its Ionian protectorate to the Kingdom of Greece, to strengthen the new King George I. British engineers demolished the Venetian fortifications of Corfu before leaving, and the flag came down on 2 June.
events.significance: It is the only case in the nineteenth century of Britain handing a European possession to another state because its inhabitants kept voting to go. It also created a precedent Greek Cypriots would quote for the next hundred years, and which Britain would refuse.

places.name: Corfu
places.note: Seat of the Lord High Commissioner; its fortresses were blown up before the handover.

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: sent in 1858 to reform the protectorate and concluded it could not be saved

people.name: Henry Storks
people.role: last Lord High Commissioner, who carried out the handover

people.name: George I of Greece
people.role: the new Danish-born king whose accession the cession was designed to support

pedagogy.hook: Britain gave away Corfu in 1864, and blew up its fortresses on the way out so that nobody else could use them.

misconception.belief: Colonies had to fight to get rid of Britain.
misconception.correction: The Ionian assembly voted for union with Greece repeatedly, Gladstone reported that no reform would satisfy them, and Britain left. What made it possible was that the islands had stopped being strategically necessary once Malta and the overland route to India mattered more. When Cypriots asked for the same treatment after 1878, Britain refused for eighty years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It sets up the Cyprus story exactly: the same demand, the same language of enosis, and the opposite answer.

evidence.author: Robert Holland and Diana Markides
evidence.work: The British and the Hellenes: Struggles for Mastery in the Eastern Mediterranean 1850-1960
evidence.supports: The cession and its long shadow over British policy in Cyprus.

events.title: The Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty
events.summary: Britain handed Heligoland to Germany and in return Germany recognised a British protectorate over Zanzibar and withdrew its claims in what became Kenya and Uganda. The agreement also drew a long stretch of the boundary between British and German East Africa.
events.significance: It is the single clearest illustration of how Africa was actually partitioned: not at the Berlin conference of 1884-85, but in bilateral bargains between European capitals, in which a North Sea island could be exchanged for authority over millions of people who were never asked.

places.name: Heligoland
places.note: Handed to Germany on 9 August 1890 after 83 years of British rule.

places.name: Zanzibar
places.note: Declared a British protectorate in November 1890 with German agreement.

people.name: Lord Salisbury
people.role: Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary who made the exchange

people.name: Leo von Caprivi
people.role: German Chancellor who signed it weeks after Bismarck's dismissal

people.name: Ali bin Said
people.role: Sultan of Zanzibar, whose state's protectorate status was settled between two European governments

pedagogy.hook: In 1890 Britain swapped a two-square-kilometre island in the North Sea for a free hand over a quarter of East Africa.

misconception.belief: Africa was carved up at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85.
misconception.correction: Berlin set procedural rules and recognised Leopold's Congo claim. The actual borders were fixed over the following twenty years in dozens of bilateral treaties like this one, and enforced on the ground by force against people who fought back. The Heligoland treaty drew part of the line that still separates Kenya from Tanzania.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It connects a European island colony to the scramble for Africa in one document, and shows the currency in which imperial bargains were paid.

evidence.author: Jan Ruger
evidence.work: Heligoland: Britain, Germany, and the Struggle for the North Sea
evidence.supports: The negotiation and terms of the exchange and the reaction in both countries.

events.title: Sette Giugno: Four Killed in Valletta
events.summary: Crowds in Valletta protesting at the price of bread and at the failure of constitutional reform attacked the offices of a pro-British newspaper and the houses of grain importers. British troops opened fire and killed four Maltese men; a fifth died later of his wounds.
events.significance: Within two years Britain granted Malta self-government, which it had refused for a century. Sette Giugno is a public holiday in Malta and one of the clearest cases in the empire of a concession arriving immediately after a shooting.

places.name: Valletta
places.note: The shootings took place in the streets around Strada Reale, now Republic Street.

people.name: Manwel Attard
people.role: one of the men shot dead by British troops on 7 June 1919

people.name: Guzeppi Bajada
people.role: killed in the same firing

people.name: Lorenzo Dyer
people.role: killed in the same firing

people.name: Karmenu Abela
people.role: bayoneted on 7 June and died of his wounds soon after

toll.note: Four men were killed on the day and a fifth died later of wounds; Maltese and British accounts differ on whether the fifth death is counted with the others.

pedagogy.hook: Four men were shot in a street in Valletta over the price of bread, and two years later Malta had its own parliament.

misconception.belief: Self-government was granted when colonies were judged ready for it.
misconception.correction: It was usually granted when refusing became expensive or dangerous. Malta had asked for constitutional reform for decades and been refused; after the shootings of June 1919 a commission was appointed within weeks and a constitution followed in 1921.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a small, precisely dated example of the pattern that runs through the whole atlas: pressure, refusal, violence, concession.

evidence.author: Henry Frendo
evidence.work: Party Politics in a Fortress Colony: The Maltese Experience
evidence.supports: The riots, the shootings and the constitutional consequences.

events.title: The Siege of Malta
events.summary: Italian and then German aircraft bombed Malta for two and a half years to destroy the base that was sinking Axis convoys to North Africa. About 1,500 civilians were killed and some 30,000 buildings destroyed; the island came within weeks of starvation before the Pedestal convoy got through.
events.significance: Malta was the most heavily bombed place on earth in 1942, and holding it kept the Mediterranean route open and cut Rommel's supplies. George VI awarded the George Cross to the whole island on 15 April 1942, the only time a decoration has been given to a population.

places.name: Grand Harbour, Valletta
places.note: Where the tanker Ohio was towed in, half sunk, on 15 August 1942 with the fuel that saved the island.

people.name: William Dobbie
people.role: Governor through the worst of the bombing until May 1942

people.name: Lord Gort
people.role: Governor from May 1942, who arrived by flying boat and cut rations to the minimum

people.name: Dudley Mason
people.role: master of the tanker Ohio, awarded the George Cross for bringing his burning ship into Grand Harbour

toll.note: About 1,500 Maltese civilians were killed by bombing, with roughly 3,700 injured, on official wartime returns; several hundred British and Commonwealth service personnel also died in the island's defence.

pedagogy.hook: In April 1942 more bombs fell on Malta than on London during the entire Blitz, and the island was awarded the George Cross — the only time a whole population has been decorated.

misconception.belief: Colonial populations were bystanders in Britain's wars.
misconception.correction: Maltese civilians lived under two and a half years of bombing to keep a British naval base working, and Maltese servicemen and dockyard workers kept it working. The George Cross is on Malta's flag today, and so is the argument about what the island got in return: within a decade Britain was running the dockyard down.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The siege explains both why Malta was fiercely loyal in 1942 and why it was voting on integration in 1956 and independence in 1964: the base was the whole relationship, and the base was ending.

evidence.author: Ernle Bradford
evidence.work: Siege: Malta 1940-1943
evidence.supports: The bombing, the convoys and the civilian experience.

events.title: The German Occupation of the Channel Islands
events.summary: Britain demilitarised the Channel Islands in June 1940 without telling Germany, evacuated about a quarter of the population, and left. German aircraft bombed St Peter Port on 28 June, killing 34 people; troops landed on Guernsey on 30 June and Jersey on 1 July, and stayed for five years.
events.significance: These were the only British territories occupied by Nazi Germany. Islanders lived under German rule administered by their own officials, about 2,000 people were deported to camps in Germany, Jewish residents were registered and three were murdered at Auschwitz, and on Alderney the SS ran a concentration camp.

places.name: St Peter Port, Guernsey
places.note: Bombed on 28 June 1940 when German aircraft mistook lorries queuing for tomatoes for troop transports.

places.name: Lager Sylt, Alderney
places.note: An SS concentration camp from March 1943, a subcamp of Neuengamme; the only one on British soil.

people.name: Alexander Coutanche
people.role: Bailiff of Jersey, who stayed and administered the island under German orders throughout

people.name: Victor Carey
people.role: Bailiff of Guernsey, who signed the orders registering the islands' Jewish residents

people.name: Therese Steiner
people.role: Austrian Jewish refugee working in Guernsey, deported in April 1942 and murdered at Auschwitz

people.name: Sibyl Hathaway
people.role: Dame of Sark, who governed the island through the occupation and confronted the German commanders in German

toll.note: The range is for deaths in the Alderney camps, as found by the expert review commissioned by the UK government and published in 2024. Separately, 34 islanders died in the bombing of June 1940 and at least 22 Channel Islanders died in Nazi camps on the continent.

pedagogy.hook: Hitler occupied British soil for five years, and the orders were carried out by British officials who stayed at their desks.

misconception.belief: Britain was never occupied, so it never faced the choices occupied Europe faced.
misconception.correction: The Channel Islands were occupied from June 1940 to May 1945. Island officials had to decide whether to enforce German orders, including the registration of Jewish residents, or resign and be replaced. Three Jewish women deported from Guernsey were murdered at Auschwitz. Historians have argued since 1995 about whether the officials had any real choice.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the one place in this atlas where British administrators were the colonised, and the questions usually asked about collaboration elsewhere in the empire are asked about them.

evidence.author: Madeleine Bunting
evidence.work: The Model Occupation: The Channel Islands under German Rule, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The occupation, the conduct of the island authorities and the postwar argument about it.

evidence.author: Paul Sanders
evidence.work: The British Channel Islands under German Occupation, 1940-1945
evidence.supports: The administration of the occupation, the deportations and the Alderney camps.

contested.note: How far the island administrations collaborated, and how many people died in the Alderney camps, are both disputed. A UK government expert review published in 2024 put the Alderney deaths at 641 to 1,027, well below some earlier claims.

events.title: The Cyprus Emergency
events.summary: EOKA, led by Colonel Georgios Grivas, began bombing British installations on 1 April 1955 to force union with Greece. Britain declared a state of emergency, detained about 3,000 people without trial, hanged nine EOKA members, and deported Archbishop Makarios to the Seychelles for over a year.
events.significance: Britain won militarily and lost politically, ending with an independence settlement it had spent four years saying was impossible. The emergency also hardened the division between Greek and Turkish Cypriots that produced the collapse of 1963 and the partition of 1974.

places.name: Nicosia
places.note: Ledra Street was nicknamed 'the Murder Mile' by British troops.

places.name: Seychelles
places.note: Where Archbishop Makarios was deported and held from March 1956 to April 1957.

people.name: Georgios Grivas
people.role: founded and commanded EOKA under the codename Digenis and was never captured

people.name: Archbishop Makarios III
people.role: political leader of the enosis campaign; deported in 1956 and later the republic's first President

people.name: Field Marshal Sir John Harding
people.role: Governor who ran the counter-insurgency and introduced detention without trial and collective punishment

people.name: Michael Karaolis
people.role: EOKA member hanged on 10 May 1956 aged 23, the first of nine executions

people.name: Fazil Kucuk
people.role: Turkish Cypriot leader who campaigned for partition against enosis
