toll.note: British counts give 371 service personnel and police dead; EOKA lost about 90 members, nine of them hanged, and killed roughly 200 Greek Cypriots as suspected informers along with Turkish Cypriot police and British civilians. No agreed total exists and the categories overlap.

pedagogy.hook: Britain deported an archbishop to the Seychelles for four hundred days, then made him president of the country three years later.

misconception.belief: Britain suppressed rebellions and then left when the rebels won.
misconception.correction: In Cyprus Britain broke EOKA's organisation militarily by 1958 and still left, because the political price of staying — a war with Greece and Turkey both interested, and a hostile United Nations — was higher than the base was worth. Then it kept the part it actually needed: 254 square kilometres of sovereign base area.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cyprus shows the late empire's real calculation. Britain did not leave when it lost; it left when the accounts stopped balancing, and it kept whatever it could carve out.

evidence.author: David French
evidence.work: Fighting EOKA: The British Counter-Insurgency Campaign on Cyprus, 1955-1959
evidence.supports: The conduct of the campaign, detention, interrogation and collective punishment.

evidence.author: Robert Holland
evidence.work: Britain and the Revolt in Cyprus, 1954-1959
evidence.supports: The politics of the emergency and the road to the Zurich and London agreements.

contested.note: Allegations of torture and ill-treatment during interrogation in Cyprus were made at the time, denied, and partly substantiated later; in 2019 the British government settled claims by 33 Greek Cypriots without admitting liability.

events.title: Malta Votes to Join Britain
events.summary: Dom Mintoff's Labour government put integration with the United Kingdom to a referendum: three Maltese MPs at Westminster, British social services and British wage rates. About 74% of those who voted said yes, but the Nationalist Party and the Catholic Church urged abstention and turnout was under 60%.
events.significance: Britain used the low turnout to avoid paying for parity of living standards, the plan collapsed by 1958, and Malta took independence in 1964 instead. It is the best-documented case in the empire of a colony asking to be let all the way in and being refused on cost.

places.name: Valletta
places.note: Where the Round Table Conference proposals of 1955 were debated and the referendum held.

people.name: Dom Mintoff
people.role: Prime Minister of Malta who proposed integration and then, when Britain would not fund it, turned to independence and to breaking with Britain entirely

people.name: Giorgio Borg Olivier
people.role: Nationalist leader who called for abstention and later negotiated independence

people.name: Michael Gonzi
people.role: Archbishop of Malta, whose opposition on church-state grounds helped depress the turnout

pedagogy.hook: In 1956 Malta voted to become part of the United Kingdom. Britain decided it could not afford Maltese people on British wages.

misconception.belief: Colonised people always wanted to be free of Britain.
misconception.correction: They wanted many different things at different times: independence, dominion status, federation, union with a neighbour, or full integration with Britain. Malta voted for integration in 1956; Gibraltarians have voted twice to stay British; Cypriots wanted union with Greece. The demand was usually for control and for equality, and independence was one route to it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the sharpest available test of whether the empire was about spreading British institutions. When a colony asked for the full set, including the wages, the answer was no.

evidence.author: Henry Frendo
evidence.work: Party Politics in a Fortress Colony: The Maltese Experience
evidence.supports: The integration campaign, the referendum and its collapse.

contested.note: Whether the referendum showed a real majority for integration is disputed: about 74% of votes cast were in favour, but on a turnout under 60% after a boycott campaign, so supporters and opponents each quote a different number.

events.title: The Annexation of Rockall
events.summary: A Royal Navy party landed by helicopter on a 25-metre granite stack 300 kilometres west of the Outer Hebrides, cemented a brass plaque to it and raised the flag, so that the Soviet Union could not observe a British guided-missile test from it. The Island of Rockall Act 1972 made it part of Inverness-shire.
events.significance: It is the last territorial expansion of the British Empire, and it happened in 1955, eight years after Indian independence. It is also a lesson in why states claim rocks: the seabed rights around Rockall are still disputed by Ireland, Denmark and Iceland.

places.name: Rockall
places.note: An uninhabited granite stack about 25 metres across and 17 metres high, annexed on 18 September 1955.

people.name: Desmond Scott
people.role: Royal Navy lieutenant commander who landed from HMS Vidal, cemented the plaque and read the proclamation

people.name: Tom Buchanan
people.role: Royal Marine sergeant who raised the Union flag on the rock

pedagogy.hook: The last territory the British Empire ever annexed was an uninhabited rock in the North Atlantic, claimed in 1955 so that the Soviet Union could not watch a missile test from it.

misconception.belief: The empire only shrank after 1945.
misconception.correction: It mostly did, but not only. Britain annexed Rockall in 1955, kept sovereign base areas in Cyprus in 1960, and in 1965 detached the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory, removing its people. Territorial claims were still being made while the flag was coming down elsewhere.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Rockall is a joke with a serious point: territory is claimed for what surrounds it — fishing, seabed, missile ranges — as much as for the land itself.

evidence.author: James Fisher
evidence.work: Rockall
evidence.supports: The 1955 annexation, the landing party and the rock itself.

evidence.author: United Kingdom Parliament
evidence.work: Island of Rockall Act 1972
evidence.supports: The incorporation of Rockall into the county of Inverness.

contested.note: The annexation of the rock itself is not disputed, but the maritime zone around it is: under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea an uninhabitable rock generates no exclusive economic zone, and Ireland, Denmark and Iceland have all contested British claims to the surrounding seabed.
